chapters.title: Welcome: How to Use This Handbook

paras.t: Welcome to the Patterns Handbook. This book is meant to be heard: on a walk, on the train, or while you cook. Each chapter explains one problem-solving pattern in plain words, tells you how to spot it, and gives you a template you can rebuild from memory.

Interview problems look endless, but most of them are a handful of ideas in disguise. Once you can name the pattern, the solution usually follows. Listen to a chapter, then open the Practice tab and solve two or three problems with that pattern while it's fresh.
A tip before we start: don't rush. Understanding why a pattern works beats memorising a hundred solutions.
Big-O notation answers one question: when the input gets bigger, how much more work does my code do?

If doubling the input doubles the work, that's linear, O of n. If it quadruples the work, that's quadratic, O of n squared, which usually means two nested loops. If the work barely grows, like binary search, which only adds one step each time the input doubles, that's logarithmic, O of log n.

Here's a practical rule. If n is around a hundred thousand, quadratic is too slow, so aim for n log n or linear. Many of the patterns in this book exist precisely to turn a nested loop into a single pass.
Two pointers means walking through data with two indexes instead of one, so one pass replaces a nested loop.

The first flavour starts the pointers at opposite ends. Picture a sorted list and a target sum. Put the left pointer on the smallest number and the right pointer on the largest. If their sum is too small, the only way to grow it is to move left forward. If it's too big, move right backward. Every step throws away a number that can never be part of the answer, so you finish in linear time.

The second flavour moves both pointers the same way: a read pointer scans everything, and a write pointer marks where the next kept value should go. That's how you remove duplicates or move zeros in place, with constant extra memory.
Spot it when you see words like sorted, pair, triple, palindrome, reverse, or in place.
A sliding window is a stretch of consecutive elements with a left edge and a right edge. Instead of recomputing every possible subarray, you slide the window and update a running summary.

Here is the template to memorise. Loop the right edge across the array. First, add the element at right to your window: add it to a sum, or bump its count in a map. Then, while the window breaks the rule, shrink it from the left: remove the element at left and move left forward. In Java, this shrink step reads nicely as a for loop with an empty start: for, semicolon, while the sum is at least s, semicolon, subtract the left value and increment left.

For a shortest-window question, record the answer inside the shrink loop, while the window is still valid. For a longest-window question, shrink until the window is valid again, then record its length. Use a sentinel like n plus one to mean "not found yet".
Why is it fast? Each element enters the window once and leaves once, so even with a loop inside a loop, the total work is linear.
Spot it with words like contiguous, substring, subarray, longest, shortest, at most k, or window of size k.

Imagine two runners on a track: one runs twice as fast as the other. If the track is a loop, the fast runner eventually laps the slow one and they meet. If the track has an end, the fast runner simply reaches it.

That's the fast and slow pointer pattern. Move slow one step and fast two steps. If they meet, there's a cycle. To find where the cycle starts, send one pointer back to the beginning and move both one step at a time; they meet exactly at the entrance.

The same trick finds the middle of a linked list: when fast reaches the end, slow is halfway. It even works on number sequences, like detecting whether repeatedly summing the squares of digits loops forever.
A hash map remembers what you've seen, with near-instant lookups. It's the most common way to trade a little memory for a lot of speed.

The classic move is the complement lookup. To find two numbers that add up to a target, walk the list once, and for each number ask: have I already seen target minus this number? If yes, you're done; if not, remember the current number.

Counting is the other big use: letter frequencies for anagrams, votes, or how many times each value appears. When the key space is small, like lowercase letters, a plain array of 26 counters is even faster.
A prefix sum is a running total: position i holds the sum of everything before it. With it, the sum of any range becomes one subtraction.

The deeper trick combines prefix sums with a hash map. To count subarrays that sum to k, keep the running total and a map of how many times each earlier total occurred. A subarray ending here sums to k exactly when an earlier total equals the current total minus k. This works even with negative numbers, where a sliding window would fail.
A cousin of this idea, the difference array, records only where values change, then rebuilds every total with one prefix sum.
Binary search halves the search space at every step, so a million items take only about twenty steps.

Beyond finding a value in a sorted array, learn the lower-bound form: find the first position where the condition becomes true. Keep a range from lo to hi; if the middle fails the condition, the answer is to the right; otherwise it's at the middle or to the left.

The most powerful use is searching over answers. If a speed, capacity or time works, then every larger one also works. Binary search the smallest value that passes a quick greedy check, such as the slowest eating speed or the smallest truck capacity.

A stack is last in, first out. It's perfect whenever the most recent unfinished thing must be handled first: matching brackets, undo operations, evaluating expressions, or walking a tree without recursion.

A monotonic stack keeps its values in sorted order. When a new value arrives, pop every value it beats; for each popped item, the newcomer is its "next greater element". Each item is pushed once and popped once, so the whole pass is linear. That's how you answer "how many days until a warmer day" or find the largest rectangle in a bar chart.
Linked list problems are about rewiring next pointers without losing the rest of the list.

Three habits make them easy. First, use a dummy node in front of the head, so you never special-case the first node. Second, when reversing, keep two pointers, previous and current, and save the next node before you flip the arrow. Third, use a gap: to remove the k-th node from the end, move one pointer k steps ahead, then walk both together until the leader reaches the end.
Draw the boxes and arrows on paper, and the code nearly writes itself.
Most tree problems are solved by asking one question: what should each node report to its parent?

For the depth of a tree, a node reports one plus the deeper of its children. For the diameter, a node reports its depth upward while updating a global best with left depth plus right depth. For a valid search tree, pass down the allowed range instead.

Level-by-level questions use a queue instead: process one level at a time, and the rightmost node of each level is what you'd see from the right side. Remember that an in-order walk of a binary search tree visits values in sorted order, which turns many tree problems into array problems.
Graphs are everywhere once you look: grids, course prerequisites, friendships, word ladders. Name the nodes and edges first.

Breadth-first search uses a queue and finds the fewest steps in unweighted graphs. Depth-first search dives deep and is great for exploring regions, like counting islands. For dependencies, topological sort repeatedly takes nodes with no remaining prerequisites; if some nodes never become free, there's a cycle.
Union-find tracks connected groups with near-constant merges. And when edges have weights, Dijkstra's algorithm always settles the closest unsettled node next, using a min-heap.

A heap hands you the smallest or largest item in logarithmic time. Whenever you hear top k, think of a min-heap of size k: push each value, and pop the smallest once the heap grows past k. Two heaps, one for the lower half and one for the upper half, track a running median.

Interval problems almost always start by sorting by start time. Then sweep: if the next interval overlaps the last one, merge; otherwise start a new one. To count meeting rooms, sort start times and end times separately and walk them with two pointers. To keep the most non-overlapping intervals, greedily keep the one that ends first.
Backtracking explores every possible choice, but abandons a path the moment it can't succeed.

The rhythm is choose, explore, un-choose. Add a candidate to the current path, recurse to decide the next position, then remove the candidate before trying the next one. That's how you generate subsets, permutations, combinations that hit a target, and solutions to puzzles like placing queens on a board.
Prune early: if a partial path already breaks a rule, stop. Good pruning turns impossible searches into fast ones.
Dynamic programming is careful reuse. When a brute-force recursion keeps solving the same smaller problems, store each answer once.

Follow four steps. Define the state: what does a single cell mean, in words? Write the transition: how does a state come from smaller ones? Set the base cases. Then identify which cell holds the final answer.

Very often you only need the last one or two values, so the table shrinks to a sliding window of a few variables, like climbing stairs or robbing houses in constant space. For two strings, a two-dimensional table compares prefixes, and keeping just two rows is enough.
A greedy algorithm makes the best-looking choice right now and never looks back. It's fast and simple, but only correct when you can argue that the local choice is always safe.

Classic examples: to reach the end of an array of jumps, track the farthest index you can reach. To keep the most meetings, pick the one that ends first. To find a starting gas station, restart whenever the tank goes negative.
Before trusting a greedy idea, try hard to break it with a tiny counterexample. If you can, switch to dynamic programming.
Interviewers judge your process as much as your answer. Here is a reliable flow.

First, restate the problem and ask about edge cases: empty input, duplicates, negative numbers, huge sizes. Second, describe a brute-force solution and its complexity, even if it's slow. Third, look for the pattern: is this a window, two pointers, a map, a heap? Explain why it helps. Fourth, write clean code with good names. Fifth, dry-run a small example out loud and fix bugs calmly. Finally, state the time and space complexity.
If you get stuck, say what you're thinking. Silence is the only truly wrong answer. Good luck. You've got this.

chapters.title: 1. Pair Sum in a Sorted List

paras.t: You get a list of integers nums sorted from smallest to largest, and a number target. Find the two different positions whose values add up to target and return them as [i, j] with i < j.
paras.s: You get a list of integers nums sorted from smallest to largest, and a number target. Find the two different positions whose values add up to target and return them as i, j with i is less than j.

paras.t: Exactly one such pair exists.
Approach: Two Pointers.
Put one pointer, L, on the smallest number and another, R, on the largest.
If their sum is too small, the only way to grow it is to move L to the right. If it is too big, move R to the left. Each step throws away one number that can never be part of the answer.
Time O(n), space O(1). Each step moves one pointer inward, so we take at most n steps and only store two indexes.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. Each step moves one pointer inward, so we take at most n steps and only store two indexes.

paras.t: A phrase counts as a palindrome if, after you ignore everything that is not a letter or a digit and treat uppercase and lowercase as equal, it reads the same forwards and backwards.
Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome under these rules.
Approach: Two Pointers.
Put L at the start and R at the end. Skip over punctuation and spaces on either side.
When both point at letters or digits, compare them ignoring case. Any mismatch means it is not a palindrome. If the pointers meet, it is.
Time O(n), space O(1). Every character is visited at most once by one of the two pointers, and we never build a cleaned copy.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. Every character is visited at most once by one of the two pointers, and we never build a cleaned copy.

paras.t: You are given an array of characters chars. Reverse it in place: modify the array itself and use only O(1) extra memory.
paras.s: You are given an array of characters chars. Reverse it in place: modify the array itself and use only O of one extra memory.

paras.t: Approach: Two Pointers.
L starts at the front and R at the back. Swap the two characters, then step both pointers toward the middle.
When they meet, every character has been swapped into its mirrored position.
Time O(n), space O(1). We do n/2 swaps and only keep two indexes.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. We do n/2 swaps and only keep two indexes.

paras.t: Rearrange the integer array nums in place so that every 0 ends up at the end, while all the non-zero numbers keep their original relative order.
Approach: Two Pointers (read & write).
paras.s: Approach: Two Pointers (read and write).

paras.t: Use a read pointer R that scans every number, and a write pointer W that marks where the next non-zero number should go.
Each time R finds a non-zero number, swap it into position W and move W forward. Zeros naturally drift to the end.
Time O(n), space O(1). R passes over the array once; each swap is constant work.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. R passes over the array once; each swap is constant work.

chapters.title: 5. Remove Repeats From a Sorted List

paras.t: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove the repeated values in place so each distinct value appears once, keeping the order. Return k, the number of distinct values; the first k slots of nums must hold them.
Approach: Two Pointers (read & write).
paras.s: Approach: Two Pointers (read and write).

paras.t: The first value is always kept, so the write pointer W starts at 1. The read pointer R scans the rest.
Whenever R sees a value different from the last kept one, copy it to W and move W forward. At the end, W is the count of distinct values.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 6. Allow Each Value At Most Twice

paras.t: nums is sorted. Remove extra copies in place so every value appears at most twice, keeping the order. Return k, the new length; the first k slots of nums must hold the result.
Approach: Two Pointers (read & write).
paras.s: Approach: Two Pointers (read and write).

paras.t: Keep a write pointer W. A value may be written if fewer than two values are written so far, or if it differs from the value two slots behind W.
That single comparison guarantees no value appears three times in a row.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 7. Merge Two Sorted Lists Into the First

paras.t: a has length m + n: its first m values are sorted and the last n slots are zeros (free space). b holds n sorted values. Merge b into a in place so that a becomes fully sorted.
paras.s: a has length m plus n: its first m values are sorted and the last n slots are zeros (free space). b holds n sorted values. Merge b into a in place so that a becomes fully sorted.

paras.t: Approach: Two Pointers from the back.
The free space is at the end of a, so fill the result from the back. I points at the last real value of a, J at the last value of b, and K at the slot to fill.
Put the larger of the two tails into slot K and move that pointer left. When b runs out, everything left in a is already in place.
Time O(m + n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of m plus n, space O of one.

paras.t: nums is sorted ascending and may contain negative numbers. Return a new array of the squares of each number, also sorted ascending.
Approach: Two Pointers.
The largest square is always at one of the two ends, because large negatives sit on the left and large positives on the right.
Compare the two ends, put the bigger square at the back of the result, and move that pointer inward. Repeat until the result is full.
Time O(n), space O(1) extra. One pass with two pointers; apart from the output we use constant space.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one extra. One pass with two pointers; apart from the output we use constant space.

paras.t: heights[i] is the height of a vertical wall at position i. Choose two walls; together with the ground they form a tank whose water level is limited by the shorter wall. Return the largest amount of water any pair can hold (width × shorter height).
paras.s: heights at i is the height of a vertical wall at position i. Choose two walls; together with the ground they form a tank whose water level is limited by the shorter wall. Return the largest amount of water any pair can hold (width times shorter height).

paras.t: Approach: Two Pointers.
Start with the widest tank: L at the first wall and R at the last. The water is limited by the shorter wall.
Moving the taller wall inward can only shrink the width without raising the limit, so always move the shorter wall. Track the best area as you go.
Time O(n), space O(1). Each step discards one wall forever, so there are at most n steps.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. Each step discards one wall forever, so there are at most n steps.

paras.t: Return every distinct triple of values [a, b, c] from nums (using three different positions) with a + b + c = 0. No triple may appear twice. Any order is accepted.
paras.s: Return every distinct triple of values a, b, c from nums (using three different positions) with a plus b plus c equals 0. No triple may appear twice. Any order is accepted.

paras.t: Approach: Sort + Two Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Two Pointers.

paras.t: Sort the array. Fix the first number of the triple, then look for two numbers to its right that add up to minus that number, using L and R from both ends.
Skip values equal to the previous one so the same triple is never reported twice.
Time O(n²), space O(1) extra. Sorting is O(n log n); for each of the n fixed values the two-pointer scan is O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n squared, space O of one extra. Sorting is O of n log n; for each of the n fixed values the two-pointer scan is O of n.

paras.t: Pick three values at different positions of nums whose sum is as close as possible to target, and return that sum. Exactly one closest sum exists.
Approach: Sort + Two Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Two Pointers.

paras.t: Sort, fix the first value, and use L and R on the remaining range. If the current sum is below the target, move L right to grow it; if above, move R left.
Remember whichever sum has been closest so far, and stop early on an exact hit.
Time O(n²), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n squared, space O of one extra.

paras.t: nums contains only 0, 1 and 2 (three colors). Sort it in place in one pass so all 0s come first, then the 1s, then the 2s, without using a library sort.
Approach: Three Pointers.
LO marks where the next 0 goes, HI where the next 2 goes, and MID scans the unknown middle.
A 0 is swapped down to LO, a 2 is swapped up to HI, and a 1 is simply skipped. Every element is placed in a single pass.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: height[i] is the height of a bar of width 1. After rain, water collects between the bars. Return how many units of water are trapped.
paras.s: height at i is the height of a bar of width 1. After rain, water collects between the bars. Return how many units of water are trapped.

paras.t: Approach: Two Pointers.
Water above a bar depends on the shorter of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest to its right.
Keep L and R at the ends with the best height seen on each side. Whichever side is lower is the bottleneck, so its water is known right now: add it and move that pointer inward.
Time O(n), space O(1). Each bar is processed once by one pointer, with four integer variables.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. Each bar is processed once by one pointer, with four integer variables.

paras.t: Return true if you can obtain s from t by deleting some (or no) characters of t without reordering the rest — in other words, if s is a subsequence of t.
paras.s: Return true if you can obtain s from t by deleting some (or no) characters of t without reordering the rest, in other words, if s is a subsequence of t.

paras.t: Approach: Two Pointers.
Pointer I tracks the next character of s we still need; pointer J scans t.
Whenever t[j] equals the needed character, I moves forward. If I reaches the end of s, every character was found in order.
paras.s: Whenever t at j equals the needed character, I moves forward. If I reaches the end of s, every character was found in order.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 15. Rotate an Array to the Right

paras.t: Rotate nums to the right by k steps in place: each value moves k positions right, wrapping around to the front. Use O(1) extra memory.
paras.s: Rotate nums to the right by k steps in place: each value moves k positions right, wrapping around to the front. Use O of one extra memory.

paras.t: Approach: Reverse Three Times.
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k values, then reverse the rest. Each reversal is a classic two-pointer swap from both ends.
The first reversal moves the last k values to the front (backwards); the next two put each part back in the right order.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: people[i] is the weight of person i. Each boat carries at most two people and at most limit total weight. Return the minimum number of boats needed to carry everyone. Nobody is heavier than limit.
paras.s: people at i is the weight of person i. Each boat carries at most two people and at most limit total weight. Return the minimum number of boats needed to carry everyone. Nobody is heavier than limit.

paras.t: Approach: Sort + Two Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Two Pointers.

paras.t: Sort the weights. The heaviest person, at R, always needs a boat. If the lightest person, at L, fits alongside, they ride together.
Either way the heaviest leaves, so each step uses one boat and moves R left (and L right when they share).
Time O(n log n), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of one extra.

paras.t: Return true if the lowercase string s can become a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
Approach: Two Pointers.
Walk inward from both ends while the characters match. At the first mismatch we must delete one of the two characters.
So check whether the rest is a palindrome after skipping the left one, or after skipping the right one.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Reverse the order of the vowels (a, e, i, o, u in either case) in the string s, leaving every other character where it is.
Approach: Two Pointers.
L walks right and R walks left, each skipping consonants. When both sit on vowels, swap them and continue.
Strings are immutable in Java and Python, so we work on a character array copy.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: In strings s and t, the character # means "backspace": it deletes the character typed before it (if any). Return true if both strings produce the same text once typed out.
Approach: Two Pointers from the end.
Scanning backwards, a # tells us to skip the next real character. So walk I down s and J down t, each time jumping to the next character that survives.
Compare the two survivors; any difference, or one string running out first, means the texts differ.
Time O(n + m), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n plus m, space O of one.

paras.t: Rearrange nums in place into the next arrangement that is larger in dictionary order (the next permutation). If nums is already the largest arrangement, rearrange it into the smallest one (sorted ascending).
Approach: Scan + Two Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Scan plus Two Pointers.

paras.t: From the right, find the first value that is smaller than the value after it; this is the digit we must bump up. Swap it with the smallest larger value on its right.
The part after it is still in descending order, so reverse it with two pointers to make it as small as possible.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: nums has n + 1 integers, each between 1 and n, so at least one value repeats. Exactly one value is repeated (possibly many times). Return it without modifying nums and using only O(1) extra memory.
paras.s: nums has n plus 1 integers, each between 1 and n, so at least one value repeats. Exactly one value is repeated (possibly many times). Return it without modifying nums and using only O of one extra memory.

paras.t: Approach: Fast & Slow Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Fast and Slow Pointers.

paras.t: Treat each value as an arrow to an index. Because two positions hold the same value, two arrows point at the same index, which creates a cycle whose entrance is the duplicate.
Move a slow pointer one hop and a fast pointer two hops until they meet. Then restart slow from the beginning and move both one hop at a time: they meet exactly at the duplicate.
Time O(n), space O(1). Floyd's cycle detection takes linear time and just two variables.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. Floyd's cycle detection takes linear time and just two variables.

chapters.title: 22. Common Values of Two Sorted Lists

paras.t: a and b are sorted ascending. Return the values they have in common, in ascending order. If a value appears several times in both lists, include it as many times as it appears in both.
Approach: Two Pointers.
Put I at the start of a and J at the start of b. If the values are equal, it is a common value: record it and move both.
Otherwise the smaller value can't appear in the other list any more, so move the pointer that sits on it.
Time O(n + m), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n plus m, space O of one extra.

paras.t: Given positive integers nums and a positive number s, return the length of the shortest contiguous run whose sum is at least s, or 0 if no run reaches it.
Approach: Sliding Window.
This is the simplest sliding window template. Move right forward and add nums[right] to the sum first.
paras.s: This is the simplest sliding window template. Move right forward and add nums at right to the sum first.

paras.t: Then, while the sum is at least s, record the window length and shrink from the left: subtract nums[left] and move left forward. The sentinel n + 1 means "no window found yet".
paras.s: Then, while the sum is at least s, record the window length and shrink from the left: subtract nums at left and move left forward. The sentinel n plus 1 means "no window found yet".

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1). right and left each move forward at most n times, so the nested loop is still linear.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. right and left each move forward at most n times, so the nested loop is still linear.

paras.t: Given a string s, return the length of the longest contiguous piece of s in which no character appears twice.
Approach: Sliding Window.
Count the characters inside the window. Add s[right] first. If it now appears twice, shrink from the left until that character's count is back to one.
paras.s: Count the characters inside the window. Add s at right first. If it now appears twice, shrink from the left until that character's count is back to one.

paras.t: The window never holds a repeat after shrinking, so its length is a candidate answer.
Time O(n), space O(1). Each character enters and leaves the window once; the count table has a fixed ASCII size.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. Each character enters and leaves the window once; the count table has a fixed ASCII size.

paras.t: Approach: Sliding Window with Jumps.
Instead of shrinking one step at a time, remember the last index where each character was seen. When s[right] was seen inside the window, jump left just past that earlier copy in one move.
paras.s: Instead of shrinking one step at a time, remember the last index where each character was seen. When s at right was seen inside the window, jump left just past that earlier copy in one move.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(k).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of k.

chapters.title: 25. Best Sum of k in a Row

paras.t: Given an integer array nums and a window size k, return the largest sum of any k consecutive numbers.
Approach: Fixed Sliding Window.
Same template with a fixed size: add nums[right] first. Once the window is longer than k, remove nums[left] and move left.
paras.s: Same template with a fixed size: add nums at right first. Once the window is longer than k, remove nums at left and move left.

paras.t: As soon as the window holds exactly k numbers, compare its sum with the best.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 26. Longest Same-Letter Run With k Changes

paras.t: s contains uppercase letters. You may change at most k characters to any other uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest run of identical letters you can create.
Approach: Sliding Window.
Inside a window, the letters we must change are all except the most common one. So a window is valid while its length minus the top count is at most k.
Add s[right], update the top count, and shrink from the left while the window needs more than k changes.
paras.s: Add s at right, update the top count, and shrink from the left while the window needs more than k changes.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Given lowercase strings p and s, return true if some contiguous part of s is a rearrangement (permutation) of p.
Approach: Fixed Sliding Window.
Count the letters of p. Slide a window of the same length over s: add s[right], and once the window is too long, remove s[left] and move left.
paras.s: Count the letters of p. Slide a window of the same length over s: add s at right, and once the window is too long, remove s at left and move left.

paras.t: Whenever the window's counts equal p's counts, the window is a permutation of p.
Time O(n), space O(1). Comparing two 26-slot tables is constant work per step.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. Comparing two 26-slot tables is constant work per step.

paras.t: Given lowercase strings s and p, return all start indices (in increasing order) of substrings of s that are anagrams of p.
Approach: Fixed Sliding Window.
Slide a window as long as p across s while maintaining letter counts. Each time the counts match p, the window's left index is an answer.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Given strings s and t, return the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t (counting duplicates). If none exists return "". The answer is unique when it exists.
Approach: Sliding Window.
Exactly the minimum-window template: need counts what t still requires and missing counts how many characters are outstanding.
Add s[right]. While nothing is missing, record the window, then give back s[left] and move left; if that breaks the cover, the shrinking stops.
paras.s: Add s at right. While nothing is missing, record the window, then give back s at left and move left; if that breaks the cover, the shrinking stops.

paras.t: Time O(n + m), space O(1). Each character enters and leaves the window at most once; the count table has a fixed alphabet size.
paras.s: Time O of n plus m, space O of one. Each character enters and leaves the window at most once; the count table has a fixed alphabet size.

paras.t: nums contains only 0s and 1s. You may flip at most k zeros into ones. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive 1s you can get.
Approach: Sliding Window.
Rephrase: find the longest window with at most k zeros, because those zeros can all be flipped.
Add nums[right] and count zeros. While there are more than k, shrink from the left.
paras.s: Add nums at right and count zeros. While there are more than k, shrink from the left.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Trees stand in a row and fruits[i] is the kind of fruit on tree i. You have two baskets, each holding one kind of fruit (any amount). Starting at any tree and moving right, you pick one fruit per tree and must stop when a tree's fruit fits in neither basket. Return the most fruits you can pick.
paras.s: Trees stand in a row and fruits at i is the kind of fruit on tree i. You have two baskets, each holding one kind of fruit (any amount). Starting at any tree and moving right, you pick one fruit per tree and must stop when a tree's fruit fits in neither basket. Return the most fruits you can pick.

paras.t: Approach: Sliding Window.
We want the longest window with at most two different kinds. Count kinds in the window with a map.
Add fruits[right]; while three kinds are inside, shrink from the left until one kind disappears.
paras.s: Add fruits at right; while three kinds are inside, shrink from the left until one kind disappears.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 32. Longest Run With At Most k Letters

paras.t: Return the length of the longest substring of s that contains at most k distinct characters.
Approach: Sliding Window.
Add s[right] to the counts. While more than k distinct characters are inside, shrink from the left until one of them disappears. Track the longest valid window.
paras.s: Add s at right to the counts. While more than k distinct characters are inside, shrink from the left until one of them disappears. Track the longest valid window.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(k).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of k.

chapters.title: 33. Count Runs With a Small Product

paras.t: Given positive integers nums and an integer k, return how many contiguous subarrays have a product strictly less than k.
Approach: Sliding Window.
Multiply in nums[right]. While the product is at least k, divide out nums[left] and move left.
paras.s: Multiply in nums at right. While the product is at least k, divide out nums at left and move left.

paras.t: Every subarray that ends at right and starts anywhere from left to right qualifies: that's right − left + 1 new ones.
paras.s: Every subarray that ends at right and starts anywhere from left to right qualifies: that's right minus left plus 1 new ones.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: A window of size k slides over nums from left to right, one position at a time. Return the maximum value inside the window at each position.
Approach: Sliding Window + Monotonic Deque.
paras.s: Approach: Sliding Window plus Monotonic Deque.

paras.t: Keep a deque of indexes whose values decrease from front to back. The front is always the current window's maximum.
When nums[right] arrives, pop smaller values off the back: they can never win again. Pop the front once it slides out of the window.
paras.s: When nums at right arrives, pop smaller values off the back: they can never win again. Pop the front once it slides out of the window.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(k). Every index is pushed and popped at most once.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of k. Every index is pushed and popped at most once.

paras.t: prices[i] is a stock's price on day i. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell to maximise profit. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profitable trade exists.
paras.s: prices at i is a stock's price on day i. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell to maximise profit. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profitable trade exists.

paras.t: Approach: Sliding Window (buy & sell).
paras.s: Approach: Sliding Window (buy and sell).

paras.t: left is the buy day and right is the sell day; together they form a window. Move right forward every day.
If right finds a cheaper price than left, the window restarts there: left jumps to right. Otherwise check the profit of the window.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Return true if nums has two equal values at positions i ≠ j with |i − j| ≤ k.
paras.s: Return true if nums has two equal values at positions i not equal to j with |i minus j| less than or equal to k.

paras.t: Approach: Sliding Window Set.
The window holds the last k values in a set. Before adding nums[right], drop nums[left] if the window would be longer than k.
paras.s: The window holds the last k values in a set. Before adding nums at right, drop nums at left if the window would be longer than k.

paras.t: If nums[right] is already in the window, its twin is at most k positions back.
paras.s: If nums at right is already in the window, its twin is at most k positions back.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(k).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of k.

paras.t: Return the largest number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) in any substring of s with length exactly k.
Approach: Fixed Sliding Window.
Add one if s[right] is a vowel. When the window grows past k, subtract one if s[left] was a vowel and move left. Keep the best count.
paras.s: Add one if s at right is a vowel. When the window grows past k, subtract one if s at left was a vowel and move left. Keep the best count.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Return the largest sum of any non-empty contiguous subarray of nums.
Approach: Sliding Window (Kadane).
Grow the window to the right and keep its sum. If the sum before adding nums[right] is negative, that prefix only drags things down, so restart the window: left jumps to right.
paras.s: Grow the window to the right and keep its sum. If the sum before adding nums at right is negative, that prefix only drags things down, so restart the window: left jumps to right.

paras.t: The best window sum seen at any point is the answer. This is Kadane's algorithm seen as a sliding window.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Cards lie in a row with point values cards. You must take exactly k cards, each time from the left end or the right end. Return the maximum total points.
Approach: Sliding Window (cards left behind).
Whatever you take from the ends, the cards you leave form one contiguous window of length n − k. So find the window of that length with the smallest sum.
paras.s: Whatever you take from the ends, the cards you leave form one contiguous window of length n minus k. So find the window of that length with the smallest sum.

paras.t: The answer is the total of all cards minus that smallest window.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 40. Most Equal Values With k Raises

paras.t: In one operation you can add 1 to any element of nums. Using at most k operations in total, return the largest possible number of equal elements.
Approach: Sort + Sliding Window.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Sliding Window.

paras.t: After sorting, try to raise every number in the window up to nums[right], the window's largest value. The cost is that value times the length, minus the window sum.
paras.s: After sorting, try to raise every number in the window up to nums at right, the window's largest value. The cost is that value times the length, minus the window sum.

paras.t: While the cost exceeds k, shrink from the left. The widest affordable window is the answer.
Time O(n log n), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of one extra.

chapters.title: 41. Runs With Exactly k Odd Numbers

paras.t: Return the number of contiguous subarrays of nums that contain exactly k odd numbers.
Approach: Sliding Window (at most k trick).
Counting windows with at most k odd numbers is the standard template: after shrinking, every window ending at right adds right − left + 1 subarrays.
paras.s: Counting windows with at most k odd numbers is the standard template: after shrinking, every window ending at right adds right minus left plus 1 subarrays.

paras.t: Windows with exactly k odd numbers are those with at most k, minus those with at most k − 1.
paras.s: Windows with exactly k odd numbers are those with at most k, minus those with at most k minus 1.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Given an unsorted integer array nums and a target, return the indices [i, j] (with i < j) of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one answer exists.
paras.s: Given an unsorted integer array nums and a target, return the indices i, j (with i is less than j) of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one answer exists.

paras.t: Approach: Hash Map.
Walk through the numbers once. For each number x, the partner we need is target − x.
paras.s: Walk through the numbers once. For each number x, the partner we need is target minus x.

paras.t: If that partner was already seen, we're done. Otherwise remember x and its index for later numbers.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Approach: Sort + Two Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Two Pointers.

paras.t: Sort the positions by their values, then run the classic two-pointer pair search from both ends of that sorted order.
We sort positions, not values, so we can still return the original indices.
Time O(n log n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of n.

paras.t: Return true if any value appears at least twice in nums, and false if every value is distinct.
Approach: Hash Set.
Scan the numbers and keep a set of values seen so far. The first time a value is already in the set, we found a repeat.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Approach: Sort + Neighbour Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Neighbour Pointers.

paras.t: Sort the numbers so equal values become neighbours. Then walk two adjacent pointers, i − 1 and i, and compare them.
paras.s: Sort the numbers so equal values become neighbours. Then walk two adjacent pointers, i minus 1 and i, and compare them.

paras.t: Time O(n log n), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of one extra.

paras.t: Return true if lowercase strings s and t use exactly the same letters the same number of times (that is, t is an anagram of s).
Approach: Counting.
Use 26 counters. Add one for every letter of s and subtract one for every letter of t. If all counters end at zero, the strings are anagrams.
Time O(n), space O(1). The counter array has a fixed size of 26, so extra space is constant.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. The counter array has a fixed size of 26, so extra space is constant.

paras.t: Group the lowercase words in words so that words made of exactly the same letters are together. Return the groups in any order (and words within a group in any order).
Approach: Hash Map with a Signature.
Give every word a signature: its letters in sorted order. Anagrams share the same signature.
Put each word into a map list under its signature; the map's lists are the groups.
Time O(n · k log k), space O(n · k).
paras.s: Time O of n times k log k, space O of n times k.

paras.t: Return the k values that appear most often in nums, in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique.
Approach: Count + Bucket Sort.
paras.s: Approach: Count plus Bucket Sort.

paras.t: Count how often each value appears. Then make buckets where bucket c holds the values that appear exactly c times.
Walk the buckets from the highest count down, collecting values until we have k of them.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Return an array res where res[i] is the product of every element of nums except nums[i]. Do it in O(n) time without division.
paras.s: Return an array res where res at i is the product of every element of nums except nums at i. Do it in O of n time without division.

paras.t: Approach: Left & Right Running Products.
paras.s: Approach: Left and Right Running Products.

paras.t: The answer at i is the product of everything to its left times everything to its right.
First sweep left to right, writing the running product of the left side into the result. Then sweep right to left with a second running product for the right side, multiplying it in.
Time O(n), space O(1) extra. Two passes; apart from the output array we only keep one running number.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one extra. Two passes; apart from the output array we only keep one running number.

paras.t: Given an unsorted array nums, return the length of the longest sequence of consecutive integers (like 4, 5, 6, 7) whose values all appear in nums. Aim for O(n).
paras.s: Given an unsorted array nums, return the length of the longest sequence of consecutive integers (like 4, 5, 6, 7) whose values all appear in nums. Aim for O of n.

paras.t: Approach: Hash Set.
Put all values in a set. A value starts a run only if the value just below it is missing.
From each start, count upward while the next value exists. Every value is counted at most once overall, so the total work is linear.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: A value appears in nums more than n / 2 times. Return it, using O(1) extra memory.
paras.s: A value appears in nums more than n divided by 2 times. Return it, using O of one extra memory.

paras.t: Approach: Boyer–Moore Voting.
paras.s: Approach: Boyer, Moore Voting.

paras.t: Keep a candidate and a counter. A matching value adds a vote; a different value removes one. When the counter hits zero, the next value becomes the new candidate.
Every removed vote cancels one majority value with one other value, and the majority has more than half, so it survives as the final candidate.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Return the index of the first character in lowercase string s that appears exactly once, or -1 if there is none.
paras.s: Return the index of the first character in lowercase string s that appears exactly once, or minus 1 if there is none.

paras.t: Approach: Two-Pass Counting.
First pass: count every letter. Second pass: return the first index whose letter has a count of exactly one.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Two strings have the same shape (they are isomorphic) if you can replace each character of s with another character, consistently and one-to-one, to obtain t. Return true if s and t have the same shape.
Approach: Two Hash Maps.
Keep a map from s letters to t letters and another map back. Walk both strings together; if either map already holds a different partner, the shapes differ.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 52. Build a Note From Magazine Letters

paras.t: Can you write the lowercase string note using letters cut from magazine, using each magazine letter at most once? Return true or false.
Approach: Counting.
Count the letters available in the magazine. Then spend one count for each letter of the note; if any count would go negative, the note can't be built.
Time O(n + m), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n plus m, space O of one.

paras.t: Return the smallest positive integer that does not appear in the unsorted array nums. Use O(n) time and O(1) extra memory (you may modify nums).
paras.s: Return the smallest positive integer that does not appear in the unsorted array nums. Use O of n time and O of one extra memory (you may modify nums).

paras.t: Approach: Index as Hash (cyclic placement).
The answer must be between 1 and n + 1. So try to place every value v from 1 to n at index v − 1 by swapping it there.
paras.s: The answer must be between 1 and n plus 1. So try to place every value v from 1 to n at index v minus 1 by swapping it there.

paras.t: Afterwards, the first index i that doesn't hold i + 1 reveals the missing positive.
paras.s: Afterwards, the first index i that doesn't hold i plus 1 reveals the missing positive.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1). Each swap puts one value in its final place, so there are at most n swaps in total.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. Each swap puts one value in its final place, so there are at most n swaps in total.

paras.t: Build a class RangeSum that is created from an integer array nums and answers many queries query(l, r): the sum of nums[l..r] inclusive. Each query must be O(1).
paras.s: Build a class Range Sum that is created from an integer array nums and answers many queries query(l, r): the sum of nums at l..r inclusive. Each query must be O of one.

paras.t: Approach: Prefix Sums.
Precompute prefix, where prefix[i] is the sum of the first i numbers. The sum of any range is then the difference of two prefix values.
paras.s: Precompute prefix, where prefix at i is the sum of the first i numbers. The sum of any range is then the difference of two prefix values.

paras.t: Building costs one pass; every query afterwards is a single subtraction.
Time O(n) build, O(1) query, space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n build, O of one query, space O of n.

paras.t: Return the number of contiguous subarrays of nums whose sum equals k. Values may be negative.
Approach: Prefix Sum + Hash Map.
paras.s: Approach: Prefix Sum plus Hash Map.

paras.t: Keep the running prefix sum. A run ending here sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals current − k.
paras.s: Keep the running prefix sum. A run ending here sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals current minus k.

paras.t: So store how many times each prefix sum has occurred, and add the count of current − k at every step. Start with prefix 0 seen once (the empty prefix).
paras.s: So store how many times each prefix sum has occurred, and add the count of current minus k at every step. Start with prefix 0 seen once (the empty prefix).

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(n). Negative numbers break the sliding window's assumption that growing the window raises the sum, which is why we need the prefix map.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n. Negative numbers break the sliding window's assumption that growing the window raises the sum, which is why we need the prefix map.

paras.t: Return the leftmost index i where the sum of the numbers strictly left of i equals the sum strictly right of i, or -1 if no such index exists.
paras.s: Return the leftmost index i where the sum of the numbers strictly left of i equals the sum strictly right of i, or minus 1 if no such index exists.

paras.t: Approach: Prefix Sum.
Compute the total once. Walking left to right, keep the sum of everything left of i; the right side is total − left − nums[i].
paras.s: Compute the total once. Walking left to right, keep the sum of everything left of i; the right side is total minus left minus nums at i.

paras.t: The first index where both sides are equal is the answer.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: nums contains only 0s and 1s. Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray with the same number of 0s and 1s.
Approach: Prefix Balance + Hash Map.
paras.s: Approach: Prefix Balance plus Hash Map.

paras.t: Treat each 1 as +1 and each 0 as −1, and keep a running balance. If the same balance shows up at two indexes, the stretch between them has equal 0s and 1s.
paras.s: Treat each 1 as plus 1 and each 0 as minus 1, and keep a running balance. If the same balance shows up at two indexes, the stretch between them has equal 0s and 1s.

paras.t: Remember the first index of each balance; the longest gap between equal balances is the answer.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

chapters.title: 58. Runs With Sum Divisible by k

paras.t: Return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays of nums whose sum is divisible by k.
Approach: Prefix Remainders.
A run's sum is divisible by k exactly when the prefix sums before and after it leave the same remainder mod k.
Count remainders as we go; each new prefix forms a valid run with every earlier prefix that had the same remainder.
Time O(n + k), space O(k).
paras.s: Time O of n plus k, space O of k.

paras.t: Flights are numbered 1 to n. Each booking [first, last, seats] reserves seats seats on every flight from first to last inclusive. Return an array where entry i is the total seats booked on flight i + 1.
paras.s: Flights are numbered 1 to n. Each booking first, last, seats reserves seats seats on every flight from first to last inclusive. Return an array where entry i is the total seats booked on flight i plus 1.

paras.t: Approach: Difference Array + Prefix Sum.
paras.s: Approach: Difference Array plus Prefix Sum.

paras.t: Instead of adding seats to every flight in a range, mark the change: add the seats at the first flight and subtract them just after the last one.
One running sum over these marks then produces every flight's total.
Time O(n + b), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n plus b, space O of n.

chapters.title: 60. Find a Value in a Sorted List

paras.t: nums is sorted ascending with distinct values. Return the index of target, or -1 if it isn't there. Your solution must run in O(log n).
paras.s: nums is sorted ascending with distinct values. Return the index of target, or minus 1 if it isn't there. Your solution must run in O of log n.

paras.t: Approach: Binary Search.
Keep a search range from LO to HI. Look at the middle value: if it is the target we're done; if it's too small the target must be to the right, otherwise to the left.
Each step throws away half of the range, so even a million values take only about twenty steps.
Time O(log n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log n, space O of one.

paras.t: nums is sorted with distinct values. Return the index of target if present; otherwise return the index where it would be inserted to keep the order. Use O(log n).
paras.s: nums is sorted with distinct values. Return the index of target if present; otherwise return the index where it would be inserted to keep the order. Use O of log n.

paras.t: Approach: Binary Search (lower bound).

We want the first position whose value is at least the target. Use a half-open range [LO, HI): if the middle value is smaller than the target, the answer is to the right; otherwise the middle might be the answer, so keep it.
paras.s: We want the first position whose value is at least the target. Use a half-open range LO, HI): if the middle value is smaller than the target, the answer is to the right; otherwise the middle might be the answer, so keep it.

paras.t: When LO meets HI, that's the insert position.
Time O(log n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 62. First and Last Position of a Value

paras.t: nums is sorted ascending (values may repeat). Return [first, last], the first and last index of target, or [-1, -1] if it does not appear. Use O(log n).
paras.s: nums is sorted ascending (values may repeat). Return first, last, the first and last index of target, or -1, -1 if it does not appear. Use O of log n.

paras.t: Approach: Two Lower-Bound Searches.
The first position of the target is the lower bound of target. The last position is one before the lower bound of target + 1.
paras.s: The first position of the target is the lower bound of target. The last position is one before the lower bound of target plus 1.

paras.t: So the same small binary search answers both questions.
Time O(log n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log n, space O of one.

paras.t: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot (for example [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] became [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Return the index of target, or -1. Use O(log n).
paras.s: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot (for example 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 became 4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2 ). Return the index of target, or minus 1. Use O of log n.

paras.t: Approach: Binary Search.
Cut the range at the middle. One of the two halves is always in sorted order, which we can tell by comparing its ends.
If the target lies within the sorted half's range, search there; otherwise search the other half.
Time O(log n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log n, space O of one.

paras.t: A sorted array of distinct values has been rotated some number of times. Return its minimum value in O(log n).
paras.s: A sorted array of distinct values has been rotated some number of times. Return its minimum value in O of log n.

paras.t: Approach: Binary Search.
Compare the middle value with the last value of the range. If the middle is bigger, the drop (and the minimum) is to the right of mid. Otherwise the minimum is at mid or to its left.
Time O(log n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log n, space O of one.

paras.t: Given a non-negative integer x, return the largest integer r with r × r ≤ x, without using any built-in power or square-root function.
paras.s: Given a non-negative integer x, return the largest integer r with r times r less than or equal to x, without using any built-in power or square-root function.

paras.t: Approach: Binary Search on the Answer.
The answer lies between 0 and x. Guess the middle: if its square fits under x, the answer is at least that big; otherwise it's smaller. Keep halving until the range closes.
Time O(log x), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log x, space O of one.

paras.t: There are piles[i] snacks in pile i. Each hour you pick one pile and eat up to k snacks from it (if it has fewer, you finish it and wait for the hour to end). Return the smallest integer speed k that lets you finish all piles within h hours.
paras.s: There are piles at i snacks in pile i. Each hour you pick one pile and eat up to k snacks from it (if it has fewer, you finish it and wait for the hour to end). Return the smallest integer speed k that lets you finish all piles within h hours.

paras.t: Approach: Binary Search on the Answer.
Faster speeds always finish sooner, so the possible speeds split into "too slow" then "fast enough". Binary search for the first speed that is fast enough.
For a guessed speed, the hours needed are the sum over piles of pile divided by speed, rounded up.
Time O(n log m), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n log m, space O of one.

paras.t: Packages with weights weights must be shipped in the given order within days days. Each day you load packages onto a truck in order until adding the next one would exceed the truck's capacity. Return the smallest capacity that ships everything on time.
Approach: Binary Search on the Answer.
Any capacity from the heaviest package up to the total weight might work, and bigger is always easier. Binary search that range.
To test a capacity, fill each day greedily and count the days used.
Time O(n log S), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n log S, space O of one.

paras.t: A peak is a value strictly greater than its neighbours (treat outside the array as −∞). Adjacent values are never equal. Return the index of any peak in O(log n). For this exercise the input has exactly one peak.
paras.s: A peak is a value strictly greater than its neighbours (treat outside the array as minus infinity ). Adjacent values are never equal. Return the index of any peak in O of log n. For this exercise the input has exactly one peak.

paras.t: Approach: Binary Search on the Slope.
Look at the middle and its right neighbour. If the slope goes up, there must be a peak to the right; if it goes down, a peak is at mid or to the left. Halve the range accordingly.
Time O(log n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log n, space O of one.

paras.t: In the m × n grid grid, each row is sorted left to right and each row's first value is greater than the previous row's last value. Return true if target is in the grid, in O(log(m·n)).
paras.s: In the m times n grid grid, each row is sorted left to right and each row's first value is greater than the previous row's last value. Return true if target is in the grid, in O of log(m times n).

paras.t: Approach: Binary Search as One List.
Read row by row, the grid is one long sorted list of m·n values. Binary search positions 0 to m·n − 1 and convert each position into a row and column.
paras.s: Read row by row, the grid is one long sorted list of m times n values. Binary search positions 0 to m times n minus 1 and convert each position into a row and column.

paras.t: Time O(log(m·n)), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log(m times n), space O of one.

paras.t: s contains only the characters ()[]{}. Return true if every opening bracket is closed by the same kind of bracket, in the correct order.
paras.s: s contains only the characters. Return true if every opening bracket is closed by the same kind of bracket, in the correct order.

paras.t: Approach: Stack.
Push every opening bracket onto a stack. A closing bracket must match the bracket on top of the stack, which we then pop.
At the end the stack must be empty, otherwise some bracket was never closed.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Design MinStack supporting push(x), pop(), top() and getMin() (the smallest value currently in the stack), each in O(1). pop, top and getMin are only called on a non-empty stack.
paras.s: Design Min Stack supporting push(x), pop, top and get Min (the smallest value currently in the stack), each in O of one. pop, top and get Min are only called on a non-empty stack.

paras.t: Approach: Stack of (value, min) pairs.
Each stack entry stores the value and the minimum of the stack at that moment, which is the smaller of the value and the previous entry's minimum.
Popping removes both together, so the entry below always knows the correct minimum.
Time O(1) per operation, space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of one per operation, space O of n.

paras.t: Evaluate an arithmetic expression written in postfix (reverse Polish) notation, given as a list of tokens. Operators are + - * /; division truncates toward zero. The expression is always valid.
Approach: Stack.
Read tokens left to right. Push numbers. An operator pops the two most recent numbers, applies itself (the first popped is the right operand), and pushes the result.
The single number left at the end is the answer.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: temps[i] is the temperature on day i. For each day, return how many days you must wait for a strictly warmer temperature, or 0 if no warmer day comes.
paras.s: temps at i is the temperature on day i. For each day, return how many days you must wait for a strictly warmer temperature, or 0 if no warmer day comes.

paras.t: Approach: Monotonic Stack.
Keep a stack of days still waiting for a warmer day; their temperatures decrease from bottom to top.
Each new day pops every waiting day that is colder, because today is their answer. Then today joins the stack and waits.
Time O(n), space O(n). Every day is pushed once and popped at most once.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n. Every day is pushed once and popped at most once.

chapters.title: 74. Next Bigger Value in a Circle

paras.t: nums is circular: after the last element comes the first. For each element, return the first strictly greater value you meet when walking forward around the circle, or -1 if there is none.
paras.s: nums is circular: after the last element comes the first. For each element, return the first strictly greater value you meet when walking forward around the circle, or minus 1 if there is none.

paras.t: Approach: Monotonic Stack (two laps).
Walk the indexes twice around the circle. Keep a stack of indexes still waiting for a bigger value; when a bigger value arrives, it answers them.
Only push indexes during the first lap, so each one waits at most one full circle.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

chapters.title: 75. Biggest Rectangle in a Bar Chart

paras.t: heights describes a bar chart with bars of width 1. Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the bars.
Approach: Monotonic Stack.
Keep a stack of bar indexes with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives, the taller bars on the stack can't extend past it, so pop them and compute their rectangles.
A popped bar's rectangle stretches from just after the new stack top to just before the current index.
Time O(n), space O(n). Each bar is pushed and popped once. A zero-height sentinel at the end flushes the stack.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n. Each bar is pushed and popped once. A zero-height sentinel at the end flushes the stack.

paras.t: An encoded string uses the rule k[text], meaning text repeated k times; groups can be nested. Return the fully expanded string. Input is always valid and digits only appear as repeat counts.
paras.s: An encoded string uses the rule k at text, meaning text repeated k times; groups can be nested. Return the fully expanded string. Input is always valid and digits only appear as repeat counts.

paras.t: Approach: Stack.
Build the current text and current number as you read. At [, push the text-so-far and the repeat count, then start fresh.
paras.s: Build the current text and current number as you read. At, push the text-so-far and the repeat count, then start fresh.

paras.t: At ], pop them back and attach the current text repeated count times to the saved text.
paras.s: At, pop them back and attach the current text repeated count times to the saved text.

paras.t: Time O(output), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of output, space O of n.

paras.t: Repeatedly delete two adjacent equal letters from the lowercase string s until no such pair remains. Return the final string (it is unique).
Approach: Two Pointers (write head).

Treat the front of a character array as a stack. The write pointer W is its top. Read each character: if it equals the character just below W, cancel the pair by moving W back; otherwise write it at W.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Approach: Stack.
Push letters onto a stack; if the incoming letter equals the top, pop instead. What remains, bottom to top, is the answer.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Given an absolute Unix-style path, return its simplest form: one / between folders, no trailing /, . means the current folder and .. goes up one level (staying at / if already at the root).
paras.s: Given an absolute Unix-style path, return its simplest form: one divided by between folders, no trailing /,. means the current folder and.. goes up one level (staying at divided by if already at the root).

paras.t: Approach: Stack.
Split the path on /. Skip empty parts and .; for .. pop the last folder if there is one; anything else is a folder name to push.
paras.s: Split the path on /. Skip empty parts and.; for.. pop the last folder if there is one; anything else is a folder name to push.

paras.t: Join the stack with / and add a leading slash.
paras.s: Join the stack with divided by and add a leading slash.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Rocks move along a line. The size is |rocks[i]|; positive moves right, negative moves left, all at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller one shatters (both shatter if equal). Return the rocks that remain, in order.
paras.s: Rocks move along a line. The size is |rocks at i|; positive moves right, negative moves left, all at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller one shatters (both shatter if equal). Return the rocks that remain, in order.

paras.t: Approach: Stack.

Survivors wait on a stack. A left-moving rock collides with right-moving rocks on top of the stack: smaller right-movers shatter and are popped; if the top is bigger, the new rock shatters; if equal, both go.
A rock that survives every collision is pushed.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Cars drive toward a destination at mile target. Car i starts at position[i] with constant speed[i]. A faster car that catches a slower one ahead joins it and moves at the slower speed, forming a convoy. A convoy meeting exactly at the destination still counts as one. Return the number of convoys that arrive.
paras.s: Cars drive toward a destination at mile target. Car i starts at position at i with constant speed at i. A faster car that catches a slower one ahead joins it and moves at the slower speed, forming a convoy. A convoy meeting exactly at the destination still counts as one. Return the number of convoys that arrive.

paras.t: Approach: Sort + Stack.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Stack.

paras.t: Sort cars by position, closest to the destination first, and compute each car's arrival time if it drove alone.
A car that would arrive no later than the convoy ahead of it catches up and merges. Otherwise it starts a new convoy; keep the convoys' arrival times on a stack.
Time O(n log n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of n.

paras.t: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list so the last node becomes the first, and return the new head.
Approach: Two Pointers (prev & cur).
paras.s: Approach: Two Pointers (prev and cur).

paras.t: Use two pointers: prev starts empty and cur starts at the head.
At each node, remember the next node, flip cur.next to point back at prev, then slide both pointers one step forward. When cur falls off the end, prev is the new head.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: a and b are heads of two sorted linked lists. Splice their nodes together into one sorted list and return its head.
Approach: Two Pointers + Dummy Head.
paras.s: Approach: Two Pointers plus Dummy Head.

paras.t: Start from a dummy node and a tail pointer. Compare the front nodes of both lists, attach the smaller one to the tail, and advance that list's pointer.
When one list runs out, attach the remainder of the other list in one step.
Time O(n + m), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n plus m, space O of one.

paras.t: Return true if the linked list starting at head contains a cycle (some node's next points back to an earlier node). In the examples, pos is the index the last node links back to (−1 means no cycle); it is not passed to your function. Use O(1) memory.
paras.s: Return true if the linked list starting at head contains a cycle (some node's next points back to an earlier node). In the examples, pos is the index the last node links back to ( minus 1 means no cycle); it is not passed to your function. Use O of one memory.

paras.t: Approach: Fast & Slow Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Fast and Slow Pointers.

paras.t: Move slow one node at a time and fast two nodes at a time. If there's no cycle, fast reaches the end.
If there is a cycle, fast laps around and must eventually land on the same node as slow.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Return the node where the cycle in the list begins, or null if there is no cycle. pos in the examples is the index the tail links back to (−1 means none) and is not passed to your function. The output shows the list read from the returned node until it repeats.
paras.s: Return the node where the cycle in the list begins, or null if there is no cycle. pos in the examples is the index the tail links back to ( minus 1 means none) and is not passed to your function. The output shows the list read from the returned node until it repeats.

paras.t: Approach: Fast & Slow Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Fast and Slow Pointers.

paras.t: First find a meeting point with slow and fast pointers. Then start one pointer at the head and one at the meeting point and move both one step at a time.
The distances work out so that they meet exactly at the loop's entrance.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Return the middle node of the linked list. If there are two middle nodes, return the second one.
Approach: Fast & Slow Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Fast and Slow Pointers.

paras.t: Move fast two steps for every one step of slow. When fast can't move any further, slow has covered half the distance and sits at the middle.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 86. Remove the k-th Node From the End

paras.t: Remove the k-th node counting from the end of the list (k = 1 is the last node) in one pass, and return the head.
paras.s: Remove the k-th node counting from the end of the list (k equals 1 is the last node) in one pass, and return the head.

paras.t: Approach: Two Pointers with a Gap.
Start both pointers at a dummy node before the head, then move fast k steps ahead. Now walk both together until fast reaches the last node.
The gap means slow stops right before the node to delete, so we just skip over it.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 87. Does the Chain Read the Same Backwards?

paras.t: Return true if the values of the linked list read the same forwards and backwards. Aim for O(1) extra memory.
paras.s: Return true if the values of the linked list read the same forwards and backwards. Aim for O of one extra memory.

paras.t: Approach: Fast & Slow + Reverse + Two Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Fast and Slow plus Reverse plus Two Pointers.

paras.t: Use slow and fast pointers to find the middle. Reverse the second half in place.
Then walk one pointer from the head and one from the reversed half, comparing values.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 88. Weave the Chain From Both Ends

paras.t: Reorder the list L0 → L1 → … → Ln in place into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 → L2 → ….
paras.s: Reorder the list L0 to L1 to... to Ln in place into L0 to Ln to L1 to Ln minus 1 to L2 to....

paras.t: Approach: Middle + Reverse + Merge.
paras.s: Approach: Middle plus Reverse plus Merge.

paras.t: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers and cut the list there. Reverse the second half.
Now weave: take one node from the front half, then one from the reversed back half, and repeat.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 89. Add Two Numbers Stored as Chains

paras.t: Two non-negative numbers are stored as linked lists of digits in reverse order (the head is the ones digit). Return their sum as a linked list in the same format.
Approach: Digit-by-Digit with Carry.
Walk both lists together, adding the two digits and the carry. Write the ones digit into a new node and carry the tens to the next step.
Keep going while either list has digits left or a carry remains.
Time O(n + m), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n plus m, space O of one extra.

chapters.title: 90. Remove Repeats From a Sorted Chain

paras.t: The linked list is sorted. Delete nodes so each value appears once, and return the head.
Approach: Single Pointer Skip.
Walk with cur. While the next node has the same value, bypass it by pointing cur.next one node further. Otherwise move on.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Regroup the list so all nodes at odd positions (1st, 3rd, …) come first, followed by the nodes at even positions, keeping the relative order within each group. Use O(1) extra space and return the head.
paras.s: Regroup the list so all nodes at odd positions (1st, 3rd,... ) come first, followed by the nodes at even positions, keeping the relative order within each group. Use O of one extra space and return the head.

paras.t: Approach: Two Pointers (odd & even chains).
paras.s: Approach: Two Pointers (odd and even chains).

paras.t: Keep two chains: odd starts at the first node and even at the second. Repeatedly link each to the node after the other, which leapfrogs them forward.
Finally connect the end of the odd chain to the head of the even chain.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 92. Rotate a Chain to the Right

paras.t: Rotate the linked list to the right by k places: the last k nodes move to the front. Return the new head.
Approach: Ring and Cut.
Find the length and the tail. Reduce k modulo the length, link the tail back to the head to form a ring, then walk to the node that should become the new tail and cut the ring after it.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Swap every two adjacent nodes of the list (by relinking nodes, not by changing values) and return the head.
Approach: Pointer Rewiring.
Keep prev just before the next pair a, b. Rewire prev → b → a → (rest), then move prev to a, which is now the second node of the swapped pair.
paras.s: Keep prev just before the next pair a, b. Rewire prev to b to a to (rest), then move prev to a, which is now the second node of the swapped pair.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Reverse the nodes of the list k at a time and return the head. If fewer than k nodes remain at the end, leave them as they are. Only relink nodes; don't change values.
Approach: Group Reversal with Two Pointers.
Keep group_prev, the node before the current group. Check that k more nodes exist; if not, stop.
paras.s: Keep group prev, the node before the current group. Check that k more nodes exist; if not, stop.

paras.t: Reverse those k nodes with the classic prev/cur two-pointer flip, then reconnect the reversed group between group_prev and the rest of the list.
paras.s: Reverse those k nodes with the classic prev/cur two-pointer flip, then reconnect the reversed group between group prev and the rest of the list.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Return the maximum depth of a binary tree: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
Approach: Recursive DFS.
An empty tree has depth 0. Otherwise a node's depth is one more than the deeper of its left and right subtrees.
Recursion asks each child the same question and combines the answers on the way back up.
Time O(n), space O(h). Every node is visited once; the call stack is as deep as the tree's height h.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h. Every node is visited once; the call stack is as deep as the tree's height h.

paras.t: Mirror the tree: swap the left and right children of every node. Return the root.
Approach: Recursive DFS.
To mirror a tree, mirror its left and right subtrees and then swap them. The recursion bottoms out at empty children.
Time O(n), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h.

paras.t: Return true if trees a and b have the same shape and the same values in the same places.
Approach: Paired DFS (two pointers).
Move a pointer through each tree in lockstep. At every step both must be empty, or both must hold the same value with identical left and right subtrees.
Time O(n), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h.

paras.t: Return true if the tree is a mirror image of itself around its center.
Approach: Mirrored Two Pointers.
Use two pointers, one walking the left half and one the right half in mirror order. The outer pair (left.left, right.right) and the inner pair (left.right, right.left) must match at every level.
Time O(n), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h.

chapters.title: 99. Read a Tree Level by Level

paras.t: Return the node values grouped by level, from top to bottom and left to right within each level.
Approach: BFS with a Queue.
Put the root in a queue. Each round, the queue holds exactly one level: pop that many nodes, record their values, and push their children for the next round.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.
