chapters.title: 100. Is It a Valid Search Tree?

paras.t: A binary search tree keeps every value in a node's left subtree strictly smaller than the node, and every value in its right subtree strictly larger. Return true if the tree satisfies this everywhere.
Approach: DFS with Bounds.
Every node must lie strictly inside a range inherited from its ancestors. The root may be anything; going left tightens the upper bound to the parent's value, going right tightens the lower bound.
Time O(n), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h.

chapters.title: 101. Lowest Common Ancestor in a Search Tree

paras.t: Given a binary search tree and two values p and q that both exist in it, return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both in its subtree (a node counts as its own ancestor).
Approach: Walk Down the Search Tree.
Start at the root. If both values are smaller, the split happens in the left subtree; if both are bigger, in the right. Otherwise this node is where the paths to p and q split, so it is the answer.
Time O(h), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of h, space O of one.

chapters.title: 102. k-th Smallest in a Search Tree

paras.t: Return the k-th smallest value (1-indexed) in a binary search tree.
Approach: Iterative In-Order.
An in-order traversal (left, node, right) of a search tree produces values in sorted order. Do it iteratively with a stack, and stop at the k-th visited node.
Time O(h + k), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of h plus k, space O of h.

paras.t: Return the diameter of a binary tree: the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path need not pass through the root.
Approach: DFS Returning Depths.
A depth-first helper returns each subtree's depth. At each node, the longest path bending through it is left depth plus right depth, so update a global best while returning the depth upward.
Time O(n), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h.

paras.t: A tree is height-balanced if, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. Return true if the tree is balanced.
Approach: DFS with an Early Exit.
A helper returns a subtree's height, or −1 if it found an imbalance anywhere below. Each node checks its children's heights once, so the whole check is a single pass.
paras.s: A helper returns a subtree's height, or minus 1 if it found an imbalance anywhere below. Each node checks its children's heights once, so the whole check is a single pass.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h.

chapters.title: 105. What You See From the Right

paras.t: Imagine standing to the right of the tree. Return the values you can see, from top to bottom: the rightmost node of every level.
Approach: BFS, Last of Each Level.
Walk the tree level by level with a queue. The last node popped in each level is the one visible from the right.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

chapters.title: 106. Root-to-Leaf Path With a Target Sum

paras.t: Return true if some path from the root down to a leaf has node values adding up to target.
Approach: DFS With a Shrinking Target.
Walk down, subtracting each node's value from the target. At a leaf, the path works if what's left is exactly zero.
Time O(n), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h.

chapters.title: 107. Two Values in a Search Tree That Sum to k

paras.t: Return true if the binary search tree contains two different nodes whose values add up to k.
Approach: In-Order + Two Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: In-Order plus Two Pointers.

paras.t: Walk the tree in order to get its values sorted. Then run two pointers from both ends: move left right when the sum is too small, right left when it is too big.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

chapters.title: 108. Rebuild a Tree From Two Walks

paras.t: preorder (node, left, right) and inorder (left, node, right) are two traversals of the same tree with distinct values. Rebuild the tree and return its root.
Approach: Divide and Conquer + Index Map.
paras.s: Approach: Divide and Conquer plus Index Map.

paras.t: Preorder lists each root before its subtrees, so we can take roots from it one by one. A root's position in the inorder list splits the remaining values into its left part and right part.
A hash map from value to inorder index makes each split instant.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

chapters.title: 109. Best Path Sum Anywhere in a Tree

paras.t: A path is any sequence of connected nodes (each used once); it need not pass through the root. Return the largest sum of values along any non-empty path.
Approach: DFS With Gains.
For every node, compute the best downward "gain" from each child, treating negative gains as zero (just don't take that branch). The best path that bends at this node is its value plus both gains.
Return upward only one branch (value plus the better gain), because a path can't fork.
Time O(n), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h.

paras.t: A node is "good" if no node on the path from the root to it has a larger value. Return the number of good nodes.
Approach: DFS Carrying the Max.
Walk down while carrying the biggest value seen on the path so far. A node is good if its value is at least that maximum; then update the maximum for its children.
Time O(n), space O(h).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of h.

chapters.title: 111. Balanced Search Tree From a Sorted List

paras.t: Build a height-balanced binary search tree from the sorted array nums. Always choose the middle element (lo + hi) / 2 (rounding down) of the current range as the root, so the answer is unique.
paras.s: Build a height-balanced binary search tree from the sorted array nums. Always choose the middle element (lo plus hi) over 2 (rounding down) of the current range as the root, so the answer is unique.

paras.t: Approach: Divide and Conquer.

The middle value splits the list into two halves of almost equal size. Make it the root, then build the left half into the left subtree and the right half into the right subtree. Balanced halves give a balanced tree.
Time O(n), space O(log n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of log n.

paras.t: Return the k-th largest value in nums (the k-th in sorted descending order, counting duplicates).
Approach: Min-Heap of Size k.
Keep a min-heap of the k largest values seen so far. When a new value arrives, push it; if the heap grows beyond k, pop the smallest.
After every value is processed, the smallest of the k largest, the heap's top, is the k-th largest.
Time O(n log k), space O(k).
paras.s: Time O of n log k, space O of k.

paras.t: Each turn, take the two heaviest stones x ≤ y and smash them: if equal both vanish, otherwise a stone of weight y − x remains. Return the weight of the last stone, or 0 if none remain.
paras.s: Each turn, take the two heaviest stones x less than or equal to y and smash them: if equal both vanish, otherwise a stone of weight y minus x remains. Return the weight of the last stone, or 0 if none remain.

paras.t: Approach: Max-Heap Simulation.
Put all stones in a max-heap (Python's heap is a min-heap, so store negatives). Repeatedly pop the two heaviest, and push back their difference if it isn't zero.
Time O(n log n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of n.

chapters.title: 114. k Closest Points to the Origin

paras.t: Given points [x, y], return the k points closest to (0, 0) by straight-line distance, in any order. The answer is unique.
paras.s: Given points x, y, return the k points closest to (0, 0) by straight-line distance, in any order. The answer is unique.

paras.t: Approach: Max-Heap of Size k.
Keep the k closest points in a max-heap keyed by squared distance. A new point that is closer than the farthest kept point replaces it.
Time O(n log k), space O(k).
paras.s: Time O of n log k, space O of k.

paras.t: lists holds the heads of k sorted linked lists. Merge them into one sorted list and return its head.
Approach: Heap of List Heads.
Put the head of every list into a min-heap. Repeatedly pop the smallest node, attach it to the result, and push that node's successor.
Time O(N log k), space O(k).
paras.s: Time O of N log k, space O of k.

paras.t: Build MedianFinder() with addNum(x) and findMedian(), the median of all numbers added so far (the average of the two middle values when the count is even).
paras.s: Build Median Finder with add Num(x) and find Median, the median of all numbers added so far (the average of the two middle values when the count is even).

paras.t: Approach: Two Heaps.
A max-heap holds the smaller half and a min-heap holds the larger half, with sizes kept equal or the small half one bigger. The median sits on top of one or both heaps.
Time O(log n) add, O(1) median, space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of log n add, O of one median, space O of n.

paras.t: A CPU runs one task per time unit. tasks lists task types (letters); two runs of the same type must be at least n units apart, and the CPU may idle. Return the minimum total time to run every task.
Approach: Counting Formula.
Lay out the most frequent task with gaps of n between its runs: that makes (top − 1) full frames of n + 1 slots, plus a final frame holding every task that ties for the top count.
paras.s: Lay out the most frequent task with gaps of n between its runs: that makes (top minus 1) full frames of n plus 1 slots, plus a final frame holding every task that ties for the top count.

paras.t: Other tasks fill the gaps. If there are more tasks than slots, there's no idling and the answer is simply the number of tasks.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Merge all overlapping intervals [start, end] and return the result sorted by start. Intervals that touch (one ends where the next starts) also merge.
paras.s: Merge all overlapping intervals start, end and return the result sorted by start. Intervals that touch (one ends where the next starts) also merge.

paras.t: Approach: Sort + Sweep.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Sweep.

paras.t: Sort by start time. Walk through: if an interval starts before (or exactly when) the last merged interval ends, extend that one; otherwise start a new merged interval.
Time O(n log n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of n.

paras.t: intervals are non-overlapping and sorted by start. Insert new and merge where needed, returning a sorted, non-overlapping list.
Approach: Three-Phase Sweep.
Copy every interval that ends before the new one starts. Then absorb every interval that overlaps, stretching the new interval. Finally add it, followed by the remaining intervals.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Return the minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest don't overlap. Intervals that only touch at an end point are fine.
Approach: Greedy by End Time.
Sort by end time and keep greedily: an interval that starts at or after the last kept end is kept; otherwise it overlaps and is removed. Ending early always leaves the most room for the rest.
Time O(n log n), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of one extra.

paras.t: Given meeting times [start, end], return true if one person can attend all of them (a meeting may start exactly when another ends).
paras.s: Given meeting times start, end, return true if one person can attend all of them (a meeting may start exactly when another ends).

paras.t: Approach: Sort + Neighbour Check.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Neighbour Check.

paras.t: Sort by start time. Any conflict must be between neighbours, so check that each meeting starts no earlier than the previous one ends.
Time O(n log n), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of one extra.

paras.t: Given meeting times [start, end], return the minimum number of rooms needed so no two overlapping meetings share a room. A room freed at time t can be reused by a meeting starting at t.
paras.s: Given meeting times start, end, return the minimum number of rooms needed so no two overlapping meetings share a room. A room freed at time t can be reused by a meeting starting at t.

paras.t: Approach: Two Pointers Over Starts and Ends.
Sort all start times and, separately, all end times. Walk the starts with one pointer; a second pointer tracks the earliest meeting still running.
If the next meeting starts before that earliest end, we need a new room; otherwise a room frees up and we reuse it.
Time O(n log n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of n.

paras.t: a and b are lists of closed intervals, each list sorted and non-overlapping. Return the intersection of the two schedules: every overlap [max start, min end] between an interval of a and an interval of b.
paras.s: a and b are lists of closed intervals, each list sorted and non-overlapping. Return the intersection of the two schedules: every overlap max start, min end between an interval of a and an interval of b.

paras.t: Approach: Two Pointers.
Point I at an interval in a and J at one in b. Their overlap, if any, runs from the later start to the earlier end.
Then advance the pointer whose interval ends first, because it can't overlap anything later in the other list.
Time O(n + m), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n plus m, space O of one extra.

chapters.title: 124. Fewest Arrows to Pop Every Balloon

paras.t: Balloons span horizontal ranges [start, end]. An arrow shot straight up at position x pops every balloon with start ≤ x ≤ end. Return the minimum number of arrows that pop all balloons.
paras.s: Balloons span horizontal ranges start, end. An arrow shot straight up at position x pops every balloon with start less than or equal to x less than or equal to end. Return the minimum number of arrows that pop all balloons.

paras.t: Approach: Greedy by End.

Sort balloons by their end. Shoot the first arrow at the end of the earliest-ending balloon; it pops every balloon that starts by then. The next balloon that starts after the arrow needs a new arrow at its own end.
Time O(n log n), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of one extra.

chapters.title: 125. First Free Slot for Two Calendars

paras.t: Two people's busy times a and b are sorted, non-overlapping intervals [start, end). Within the working day [day_start, day_end), return the earliest slot [t, t + duration] when both are free, or [] if none exists.
paras.s: Two people's busy times a and b are sorted, non-overlapping intervals start, end). Within the working day day start, day end), return the earliest slot t, t plus duration when both are free, or if none exists.

paras.t: Approach: Two-Pointer Merge.
Walk both busy lists like a merge, always taking the interval that starts first. Keep free_from, the moment everyone is free again.
paras.s: Walk both busy lists like a merge, always taking the interval that starts first. Keep free from, the moment everyone is free again.

paras.t: If the next busy interval starts at least duration after free_from, that gap is the answer. Otherwise push free_from past it. At the end, check the gap before the day ends.
paras.s: If the next busy interval starts at least duration after free from, that gap is the answer. Otherwise push free from past it. At the end, check the gap before the day ends.

paras.t: Time O(n + m), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n plus m, space O of one.

paras.t: grid is a map of "1" (land) and "0" (water). An island is land connected up, down, left or right. Return the number of islands. You may modify the grid.
Approach: DFS Flood Fill.
Scan every cell. When you hit land, that's a new island: count it, then run a depth-first search that turns the whole connected island into water so it won't be counted again.
Time O(m · n), space O(m · n). Each cell is sunk at most once; the recursion can go as deep as the island's size.
paras.s: Time O of m times n, space O of m times n. Each cell is sunk at most once; the recursion can go as deep as the island's size.

paras.t: grid contains 1 for land and 0 for water. Return the area (number of cells) of the largest island, where cells connect up, down, left and right, or 0 if there is no land.
Approach: DFS Returning Area.
A depth-first search from a land cell sinks the island and returns how many cells it sank: 1 plus the areas found in the four directions. Keep the biggest.
Time O(m · n), space O(m · n).
paras.s: Time O of m times n, space O of m times n.

paras.t: image[r][c] is a pixel color. Starting from pixel (sr, sc), repaint it and every pixel of the same original color connected to it (up, down, left, right) with color. Return the image.
paras.s: image at r, c is a pixel color. Starting from pixel (sr, sc), repaint it and every pixel of the same original color connected to it (up, down, left, right) with color. Return the image.

paras.t: Approach: DFS.
Remember the starting color. Recursively repaint a pixel if it still has that color, then spread to its four neighbours. If the new color equals the old one, there's nothing to do.
Time O(m · n), space O(m · n).
paras.s: Time O of m times n, space O of m times n.

paras.t: In grid, 0 is empty, 1 is fresh fruit and 2 is rotten fruit. Every minute, fresh fruit next to rotten fruit (up, down, left, right) becomes rotten. Return the minutes until no fresh fruit remains, or -1 if that never happens.
paras.s: In grid, 0 is empty, 1 is fresh fruit and 2 is rotten fruit. Every minute, fresh fruit next to rotten fruit (up, down, left, right) becomes rotten. Return the minutes until no fresh fruit remains, or minus 1 if that never happens.

paras.t: Approach: Multi-Source BFS.
Put every rotten fruit in the queue at minute 0. Process the queue one minute (one level) at a time, rotting fresh neighbours and adding them for the next minute.
If fresh fruit remains when the queue empties, some fruit can never be reached.
Time O(m · n), space O(m · n).
paras.s: Time O of m times n, space O of m times n.

paras.t: There are n courses numbered 0..n−1. Each pair [a, b] in prereqs means course b must be taken before course a. Return true if it's possible to finish every course (no circular requirements).
paras.s: There are n courses numbered 0..n minus 1. Each pair a, b in prereqs means course b must be taken before course a. Return true if it's possible to finish every course (no circular requirements).

paras.t: Approach: Kahn's Topological Sort.
Count each course's unmet prerequisites. Courses with none can be taken now: put them in a queue. Taking a course reduces the count of every course that depends on it, possibly freeing new ones.
If every course eventually gets taken, there's no cycle.
Time O(V + E), space O(V + E).
paras.s: Time O of V plus E, space O of V plus E.

paras.t: Same setup: n courses and pairs [a, b] meaning b comes before a. Return an order that takes every course, always choosing the smallest-numbered available course next (so the answer is unique), or [] if impossible.
paras.s: Same setup: n courses and pairs a, b meaning b comes before a. Return an order that takes every course, always choosing the smallest-numbered available course next (so the answer is unique), or if impossible.

paras.t: Approach: Kahn's Algorithm with a Min-Heap.
Run Kahn's topological sort, but keep the available courses in a min-heap so the smallest number always goes next. If fewer than n courses come out, there's a cycle.
Time O((V + E) log V), space O(V + E).
paras.s: Time O of (V plus E) log V, space O of V plus E.

paras.t: Each Node has a value and a list of neighbors. Given one node of a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the whole graph. In the examples the graph is shown as an adjacency list where node i + 1 is at index i.
paras.s: Each Node has a value and a list of neighbors. Given one node of a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the whole graph. In the examples the graph is shown as an adjacency list where node i plus 1 is at index i.

paras.t: Approach: BFS + Copy Map.
paras.s: Approach: BFS plus Copy Map.

paras.t: Keep a map from original nodes to their copies. BFS from the start node: for every neighbour, create its copy the first time you see it, then connect the copies.
Time O(V + E), space O(V).
paras.s: Time O of V plus E, space O of V.

paras.t: Transform begin into end by changing one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in words. Return the number of words in the shortest such sequence (including begin and end), or 0 if impossible.
Approach: BFS Over Words.

Breadth-first search explores words in order of distance from begin. From each word, try changing every letter to every other letter; unvisited dictionary words go into the queue one step further away.
The first time we reach end, the step count is minimal.
Time O(n · L · 26), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n times L times 26, space O of n.

chapters.title: 134. The Link That Makes a Loop

paras.t: A tree of n nodes (labelled 1..n) got one extra edge, creating exactly one cycle. edges lists all edges. Return the edge that can be removed to make it a tree again; if several work, return the one that appears last.
Approach: Union-Find.
Union-find tracks which nodes are already connected. Add edges in order: if both ends already share a root, this edge closes the cycle, so it's the answer. Otherwise merge their groups.
Time O(n · α(n)), space O(n). With path compression each find is nearly constant time.
paras.s: Time O of n times alpha (n), space O of n. With path compression each find is nearly constant time.

chapters.title: 135. How Long Until Every Server Hears?

paras.t: times[i] = [u, v, w] means a signal sent from server u reaches server v after w milliseconds (one-way). Servers are labelled 1..n. A signal starts at server k. Return how long until every server has received it, or -1 if some server never does.
paras.s: times at i equals u, v, w means a signal sent from server u reaches server v after w milliseconds (one-way). Servers are labelled 1..n. A signal starts at server k. Return how long until every server has received it, or minus 1 if some server never does.

paras.t: Approach: Dijkstra.
Always settle the closest unsettled server next, using a min-heap of (time, server). When a server is settled, its time is final; relax its outgoing links.
The answer is the largest settled time, or −1 if some server was never reached.
paras.s: The answer is the largest settled time, or minus 1 if some server was never reached.

paras.t: Time O(E log V), space O(V + E).
paras.s: Time O of E log V, space O of V plus E.

paras.t: nums has distinct integers. Return every possible subset (the power set), in any order, with no duplicates.
Approach: Backtracking.
Build subsets one decision at a time. At each step record the current subset, then try adding each remaining element, explore deeper, and remove it again (backtrack) before trying the next one.
Time O(n · 2ⁿ), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n times 2 to the n, space O of n.

paras.t: nums has distinct integers. Return every permutation (ordering) of nums, in any order.
Approach: Backtracking with Swaps.

Fix one position at a time. For position first, swap each candidate from the rest of the array into place, recurse on the next position, then swap it back. When all positions are fixed, record the ordering.
Time O(n · n!), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n times n factorial, space O of n.

paras.t: candidates are distinct positive integers. Return every unique combination that sums to target, where each candidate may be used any number of times. Order inside a combination doesn't matter.
Approach: Backtracking.

Pick candidates in non-decreasing index order so each combination is built exactly once. Keep subtracting from the remaining target; at zero record the combination, below zero stop exploring that branch.
Time O(n^(t/min)), space O(t/min).
paras.s: Time O of n to the power of t over min), space O of t over min.

paras.t: Return every string made of n pairs of parentheses that is correctly balanced, in any order.
Approach: Backtracking With Counts.
Build the string left to right. You may add ( while fewer than n are open, and ) only while it closes an unmatched (. Those two rules generate exactly the balanced strings.
Time O(4ⁿ / √n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of 4 to the n over the square root of n, space O of n.

paras.t: On a phone keypad 2→abc, 3→def, 4→ghi, 5→jkl, 6→mno, 7→pqrs, 8→tuv, 9→wxyz. Given digits (2–9), return every letter string they could spell, in any order (empty input gives an empty list).
paras.s: On a phone keypad 2 to abc, 3 to def, 4 to ghi, 5 to jkl, 6 to mno, 7 to pqrs, 8 to tuv, 9 to wxyz. Given digits (2 to 9), return every letter string they could spell, in any order (empty input gives an empty list).

paras.t: Approach: Backtracking.
Handle one digit per level: for each letter of the current digit, append it and recurse into the next digit. When every digit has a letter, record the word.
Time O(4ⁿ · n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of 4 to the n times n, space O of n.

chapters.title: 141. Find a Word in a Letter Grid

paras.t: Return true if word can be traced in board through horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, using each cell at most once.
Approach: DFS Backtracking.

From each cell that matches the first letter, explore neighbours that match the next letter. Temporarily mark the current cell as used so the path never revisits it, and restore it when you backtrack.
Time O(m · n · 4^L), space O(L).
paras.s: Time O of m times n times 4 to the L, space O of L.

paras.t: Count the ways to place n queens on an n × n chessboard so that no two attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal).
paras.s: Count the ways to place n queens on an n times n chessboard so that no two attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal).

paras.t: Approach: Row-by-Row Backtracking.
Put exactly one queen in each row. For row r, try every column whose column, r − c diagonal and r + c anti-diagonal are all free. Record them, recurse to the next row, and free them on the way back.
paras.s: Put exactly one queen in each row. For row r, try every column whose column, r minus c diagonal and r plus c anti-diagonal are all free. Record them, recurse to the next row, and free them on the way back.

paras.t: Time O(n!), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n factorial, space O of n.

paras.t: You climb a staircase of n steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways reach the top?
Approach: Rolling Window of Two.
Ways to reach step i = ways to reach step i − 1 + ways to reach step i − 2. Instead of a whole table, slide a window of the last two answers forward.
paras.s: Ways to reach step i equals ways to reach step i minus 1 plus ways to reach step i minus 2. Instead of a whole table, slide a window of the last two answers forward.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1). This is the Fibonacci recurrence; the two-value window makes the space constant.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one. This is the Fibonacci recurrence; the two-value window makes the space constant.

paras.t: cost[i] is what you pay to stand on step i, after which you may climb 1 or 2 steps. You can start on step 0 or step 1. Return the minimum cost to get past the last step.
paras.s: cost at i is what you pay to stand on step i, after which you may climb 1 or 2 steps. You can start on step 0 or step 1. Return the minimum cost to get past the last step.

paras.t: Approach: Rolling Window of Two.

The cheapest way to stand on a step is its cost plus the cheaper of the two steps below it. Keep only those last two values and roll them forward. The top is reached from either of the last two steps.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Houses on a street hold nums[i] money. You can't take from two adjacent houses. Return the most money you can take.
paras.s: Houses on a street hold nums at i money. You can't take from two adjacent houses. Return the most money you can take.

paras.t: Approach: Rolling Window of Two.
For each house, the best total is either the best up to the previous house (skip this one), or this house plus the best up to two houses back. Two rolling values are enough.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 146. Rob Houses Arranged in a Circle

paras.t: Same as before, but the houses form a circle: the first and last houses are neighbours. Return the most money you can take.
Approach: Two Linear Passes.
Since the first and last houses can't both be robbed, solve the straight-line version twice: once without the first house and once without the last. Take the better answer.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Using unlimited coins of the given denominations, return the fewest coins that add up to amount, or -1 if it can't be made.
paras.s: Using unlimited coins of the given denominations, return the fewest coins that add up to amount, or minus 1 if it can't be made.

paras.t: Approach: Bottom-Up DP.
Let best[a] be the fewest coins making amount a, with best[0] = 0. For every amount, try finishing with each coin: one coin plus the best way to make the rest.
paras.s: Let best at a be the fewest coins making amount a, with best at 0 equals 0. For every amount, try finishing with each coin: one coin plus the best way to make the rest.

paras.t: Amounts that can't be made keep an "infinity" marker of amount + 1.
paras.s: Amounts that can't be made keep an "infinity" marker of amount plus 1.

paras.t: Time O(amount · coins), space O(amount).
paras.s: Time O of amount times coins, space O of amount.

paras.t: Return the number of different combinations of coins (unlimited supply, order doesn't matter) that make amount.
Approach: Unbounded Knapsack.
ways[a] counts combinations for amount a, with ways[0] = 1. Process one coin at a time: for every amount from the coin upward, add ways[a − coin].
paras.s: ways at a counts combinations for amount a, with ways at 0 equals 1. Process one coin at a time: for every amount from the coin upward, add ways at a minus coin.

paras.t: Putting coins in the outer loop means each combination is built in one fixed coin order, so it's never counted twice.
Time O(amount · coins), space O(amount).
paras.s: Time O of amount times coins, space O of amount.

paras.t: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of nums (elements in order, not necessarily adjacent).
Approach: Tails + Binary Search.
paras.s: Approach: Tails plus Binary Search.

paras.t: tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of a rising subsequence of length k + 1. For each number, binary search the first tail that is at least as big and replace it, or append if the number is bigger than every tail.
paras.s: tails at k is the smallest possible last value of a rising subsequence of length k plus 1. For each number, binary search the first tail that is at least as big and replace it, or append if the number is bigger than every tail.

paras.t: The number of tails is the answer. (tails itself is not necessarily a real subsequence.)
Time O(n log n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of n.

paras.t: Return the length of the longest subsequence that appears in both strings a and b.
Approach: 2D DP With Rolling Rows.
dp[i][j] is the answer for the first i letters of a and first j of b. Matching letters add one to the diagonal value; otherwise take the better of dropping a letter from either string.
paras.s: dp at i, j is the answer for the first i letters of a and first j of b. Matching letters add one to the diagonal value; otherwise take the better of dropping a letter from either string.

paras.t: Each row only needs the row above, so two rows suffice.
Time O(m · n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of m times n, space O of n.

paras.t: Return the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions or replacements that turn a into b.
Approach: 2D DP With Rolling Rows.
If the current letters match, no edit is needed: copy the diagonal. Otherwise take 1 + the cheapest of replace (diagonal), delete (above) or insert (left).
paras.s: If the current letters match, no edit is needed: copy the diagonal. Otherwise take 1 plus the cheapest of replace (diagonal), delete (above) or insert (left).

paras.t: Only the previous row is needed to compute the next one.
Time O(m · n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of m times n, space O of n.

paras.t: Return true if s can be split into a sequence of one or more words from words (words may be reused).
Approach: DP Over Prefixes.
ok[i] says the first i characters split cleanly, with ok[0] = true. Position i is reachable if some earlier reachable position j has s[j:i] in the dictionary.
paras.s: ok at i says the first i characters split cleanly, with ok at 0 equals true. Position i is reachable if some earlier reachable position j has s j:i in the dictionary.

paras.t: Time O(n²), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n squared, space O of n.

chapters.title: 153. Ways to Decode a Digit String

paras.t: Letters are encoded as 1 → A, 2 → B, …, 26 → Z. Return the number of ways to decode the digit string s.
paras.s: Letters are encoded as 1 to A, 2 to B,..., 26 to Z. Return the number of ways to decode the digit string s.

paras.t: Approach: Rolling Window of Two.
Ways to decode the first i digits = ways for i − 1 (if digit i is 1–9) plus ways for i − 2 (if the last two digits form 10–26). Keep a rolling window of the last two counts.
paras.s: Ways to decode the first i digits equals ways for i minus 1 (if digit i is 1 to 9) plus ways for i minus 2 (if the last two digits form 10 to 26). Keep a rolling window of the last two counts.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Return true if nums (positive integers) can be split into two groups with equal sums.
Approach: Reachable Sums.
If the total is odd it's impossible. Otherwise we need a subset summing to half. Keep the set of sums reachable so far; each number adds itself to every reachable sum.
Time O(n · sum), space O(sum).
paras.s: Time O of n times sum, space O of sum.

paras.t: Return the largest product of any non-empty contiguous subarray of nums.
Approach: Rolling Max and Min.

Track the largest and smallest product of a run ending at the current number. Multiplying by a negative swaps their roles, so compute both from the previous pair (or start fresh at the number itself).
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Return the longest contiguous substring of s that reads the same forwards and backwards. If several have the maximum length, return the one that starts first.
Approach: Expand Around Center (Two Pointers).
Every palindrome mirrors around a center, which is either one character or the gap between two characters. From each of the 2n − 1 centers, move left and right outward while the characters match.
paras.s: Every palindrome mirrors around a center, which is either one character or the gap between two characters. From each of the 2n minus 1 centers, move left and right outward while the characters match.

paras.t: Keep the longest stretch found.
Time O(n²), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n squared, space O of one.

paras.t: Return how many substrings of s are palindromes (substrings at different positions count separately).
Approach: Expand Around Center (Two Pointers).
From each of the 2n − 1 centers, move left and right outward. Every step where the characters still match reveals one more palindrome.
paras.s: From each of the 2n minus 1 centers, move left and right outward. Every step where the characters still match reveals one more palindrome.

paras.t: Time O(n²), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n squared, space O of one.

paras.t: A robot starts at the top-left of an m × n grid and may only move right or down. How many paths reach the bottom-right corner?
paras.s: A robot starts at the top-left of an m times n grid and may only move right or down. How many paths reach the bottom-right corner?

paras.t: Approach: 1D Rolling Row.

The number of paths to a cell is the sum of paths to the cell above and the cell to the left. Keep a single row: updating it left to right turns the old value (above) plus the new left value into the new count.
Time O(m · n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of m times n, space O of n.

chapters.title: 159. Can You Hop to the End?

paras.t: You start at index 0. nums[i] is the farthest jump length from index i. Return true if you can reach the last index.
paras.s: You start at index 0. nums at i is the farthest jump length from index i. Return true if you can reach the last index.

paras.t: Approach: Greedy Reach.
Walk left to right keeping reach, the farthest index you can get to. If you ever stand on an index beyond reach, you're stuck. Otherwise extend reach with i + nums[i].
paras.s: Walk left to right keeping reach, the farthest index you can get to. If you ever stand on an index beyond reach, you're stuck. Otherwise extend reach with i plus nums at i.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Same setup as before, but the last index is always reachable. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach it.
Approach: Window of Reachable Indices.

The indices reachable with the same number of jumps form a window. Scan the current window while tracking the farthest index the next jump could reach. When you finish a window, take one jump: the next window ends at that farthest point.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 161. Where to Start a Fuel Loop

paras.t: Stations stand in a circle. At station i you may fill gas[i] units; driving to the next station costs cost[i]. Starting with an empty tank, return the station index from which you can drive the whole loop once, or -1 if impossible. The answer is unique when it exists.
paras.s: Stations stand in a circle. At station i you may fill gas at i units; driving to the next station costs cost at i. Starting with an empty tank, return the station index from which you can drive the whole loop once, or minus 1 if impossible. The answer is unique when it exists.

paras.t: Approach: Greedy Restart.

If total gas is less than total cost, no start works. Otherwise drive from a candidate start; whenever the tank goes negative at station i, no station between the start and i can work either, so restart from i + 1 with an empty tank.
paras.s: If total gas is less than total cost, no start works. Otherwise drive from a candidate start; whenever the tank goes negative at station i, no station between the start and i can work either, so restart from i plus 1 with an empty tank.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 162. Split So Each Letter Stays in One Part

paras.t: Split the lowercase string s into as many parts as possible so every letter appears in at most one part. Return the sizes of the parts in order.
Approach: Two Pointers With Last Positions.
Record where each letter appears last. Grow the current part with a right pointer; the part must stretch at least to the last position of every letter it contains (end).
When right reaches end, close the part, record its size, and start the next part at left = right + 1.
paras.s: When right reaches end, close the part, record its size, and start the next part at left equals right plus 1.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Child i is content with a cookie of size at least greed[i]; cookie j has size sizes[j]. Each child gets at most one cookie. Return the maximum number of content children.
paras.s: Child i is content with a cookie of size at least greed at i; cookie j has size sizes at j. Each child gets at most one cookie. Return the maximum number of content children.

paras.t: Approach: Sort + Two Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Sort plus Two Pointers.

paras.t: Sort children by greed and cookies by size. Pointer child waits for a cookie; pointer cookie scans sizes. If the cookie is big enough, the child is happy and both move; otherwise the cookie is too small for anyone left and is skipped.
Time O(n log n), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n log n, space O of one extra.

paras.t: Every value in nums appears exactly twice, except one value that appears once. Return it using O(1) extra memory.
paras.s: Every value in nums appears exactly twice, except one value that appears once. Return it using O of one extra memory.

paras.t: Approach: XOR Everything.
XOR has two handy rules: a value XOR itself is 0, and XOR with 0 changes nothing. XOR-ing every number cancels all the twins, leaving only the lone number.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Return how many 1 bits the binary form of the non-negative integer n has.
Approach: Clear the Lowest Bit.
Subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 bit and every 0 below it, so n & (n − 1) removes exactly one 1 bit. Count how many times you can do that before n reaches 0.
paras.s: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 bit and every 0 below it, so n and (n minus 1) removes exactly one 1 bit. Count how many times you can do that before n reaches 0.

paras.t: Time O(number of 1 bits), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of number of one bits, space O of one.

paras.t: Return an array where entry i is the number of 1 bits in i, for every i from 0 to n.
Approach: Reuse Smaller Answers.
Shifting i right by one drops its last bit, so bits(i) = bits(i ÷ 2) + (i's last bit). Every answer reuses one we already computed.
paras.s: Shifting i right by one drops its last bit, so bits(i) equals bits(i divided by 2) plus (i's last bit). Every answer reuses one we already computed.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: nums contains n distinct numbers from the range 0..n, so exactly one number of the range is missing. Return it.
Approach: Expected Sum.
Every index 0 to n − 1 and the extra number n should cancel against the values. Add each index and subtract each value; whatever is left over is the missing number.
paras.s: Every index 0 to n minus 1 and the extra number n should cancel against the values. Add each index and subtract each value; whatever is left over is the missing number.

paras.t: This avoids computing a large sum, so it never overflows.
Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 168. Is It a Power of Two?

paras.t: Return true if the integer n equals 2^k for some integer k ≥ 0.
paras.s: Return true if the integer n equals 2 to the power of k for some integer k greater than or equal to 0.

paras.t: Approach: One Bit Set.
A positive power of two has exactly one 1 bit. Clearing the lowest 1 bit with n & (n − 1) must therefore leave zero.
paras.s: A positive power of two has exactly one 1 bit. Clearing the lowest 1 bit with n and (n minus 1) must therefore leave zero.

paras.t: Time O(1), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of one, space O of one.

paras.t: Return a + b for 32-bit signed integers without using + or -.
paras.s: Return a plus b for 32-bit signed integers without using plus or -.

paras.t: Approach: XOR + Carry.
paras.s: Approach: XOR plus Carry.

paras.t: XOR adds each bit pair while ignoring carries; AND shifted left by one gives exactly the carries. Keep adding the carries back in until none are left.
Python integers are unbounded, so we mask to 32 bits and convert back to a signed number at the end.
Time O(32), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of 32, space O of one.

paras.t: Reverse the digits of the 32-bit signed integer x. If the result falls outside the 32-bit signed range, return 0.
Approach: Pop and Push Digits.
Repeatedly take the last digit of x and append it to the result. Before appending, check that the result times 10 won't leave the 32-bit range.
Time O(log x), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log x, space O of one.

paras.t: Starting from n, repeatedly replace the number with the sum of the squares of its digits. Return true if this eventually reaches 1, and false if it loops forever without reaching 1.
Approach: Fast & Slow Pointers.
paras.s: Approach: Fast and Slow Pointers.

paras.t: Treat the chain like a linked list. Move slow one step and fast two steps. If there's a cycle they meet; if the chain reaches 1, fast gets there first (1 maps to itself).
Time O(log n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 172. Does the Number Read the Same Backwards?

paras.t: Return true if the integer x reads the same forwards and backwards, without converting it to a string.
Approach: Reverse Half the Digits.

Peel digits off the end into a reversed half until the reversed half is at least as big as what's left. Then the two halves meet in the middle, like two pointers: they must be equal (or equal after dropping the middle digit).
Time O(log x), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log x, space O of one.

paras.t: Compute x raised to the integer power n (n may be negative) in O(log |n|) multiplications.
paras.s: Compute x raised to the integer power n (n may be negative) in O of log |n| multiplications.

paras.t: Approach: Binary Exponentiation.
Look at n in binary. Square the base each step; whenever the current bit of n is 1, multiply that power into the result. A negative exponent just means using 1/x.
Time O(log n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of log n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 174. Rotate an Image a Quarter Turn

paras.t: Rotate the n × n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place.
paras.s: Rotate the n times n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place.

paras.t: Approach: Transpose + Reverse Rows.
paras.s: Approach: Transpose plus Reverse Rows.

paras.t: Swap every element across the main diagonal (rows become columns). Then reverse each row with two pointers. Together these two flips equal a clockwise quarter turn.
Time O(n²), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n squared, space O of one.

chapters.title: 175. Read a Matrix in a Spiral

paras.t: Return all elements of the m × n matrix in clockwise spiral order, starting at the top-left.
paras.s: Return all elements of the m times n matrix in clockwise spiral order, starting at the top-left.

paras.t: Approach: Four Shrinking Boundaries.

Keep four pointers: top, bottom, left and right. Read the top row left to right, then the right column downwards, then the bottom row right to left, then the left column upwards. Each edge read moves its boundary inward.
Time O(m · n), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of m times n, space O of one extra.

chapters.title: 176. Spread Zeros to Rows and Columns

paras.t: If an element of the matrix is 0, set its whole row and column to 0. Do it in place with O(1) extra memory.
paras.s: If an element of the matrix is 0, set its whole row and column to 0. Do it in place with O of one extra memory.

paras.t: Approach: First Row and Column as Markers.
Use the first cell of each row and column as a "this line must become zero" flag. Remember separately whether the first row and first column contained a zero themselves.
Then zero cells by checking their row and column flags, and finally handle the first row and column.
Time O(m · n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of m times n, space O of one.

chapters.title: 177. Search a Row- and Column-Sorted Grid

paras.t: Every row of grid is sorted left to right and every column top to bottom. Return true if target is in it.
Approach: Staircase Walk (two pointers).

Start at the top-right corner with a row pointer and a column pointer. Everything to the left is smaller and everything below is bigger. If the value is too big, move left; if too small, move down. Each step rules out a whole row or column.
Time O(m + n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of m plus n, space O of one.

paras.t: Implement Trie() with insert(word), search(word) (was this exact word inserted?) and startsWith(prefix) (was any word with this prefix inserted?). Words are lowercase.
paras.s: Implement Trie with insert(word), search(word) (was this exact word inserted?) and starts With(prefix) (was any word with this prefix inserted?). Words are lowercase.

paras.t: Approach: Nested Child Maps.
Each node holds a map from letter to child node and a flag marking the end of a word. Inserting walks (and creates) one node per letter; searching walks the same path and checks the flag at the end.
Autocomplete, spell checkers and tokenizer vocabularies use tries.
Time O(L) per call, space O(total letters).
paras.s: Time O of L per call, space O of total letters.

paras.t: Implement WordDictionary() with addWord(word) and search(pattern), where . in the pattern matches any one letter. Words are lowercase.
paras.s: Implement Word Dictionary with add Word(word) and search(pattern), where. in the pattern matches any one letter. Words are lowercase.

paras.t: Approach: Trie + DFS.
paras.s: Approach: Trie plus DFS.

paras.t: Store words in a trie. Searching follows letters normally; at a ., branch into every child and succeed if any branch matches the rest of the pattern.
paras.s: Store words in a trie. Searching follows letters normally; at a., branch into every child and succeed if any branch matches the rest of the pattern.

paras.t: Time O(26^dots · L), space O(total letters).
paras.s: Time O of 26 to the dots times L, space O of total letters.

paras.t: MovingAverage(size) receives numbers one at a time with next(val) and returns the average of the last size values (or of all values while fewer than size have arrived).
paras.s: Moving Average(size) receives numbers one at a time with next(val) and returns the average of the last size values (or of all values while fewer than size have arrived).

paras.t: Approach: Sliding Window Queue.
Keep the last size values in a queue with their running sum. Add the new value on the right; if the window is too long, remove the oldest value from the left and subtract it.
Time O(1) per call, space O(size).
paras.s: Time O of one per call, space O of size.

chapters.title: 181. Hits in the Last Five Minutes

paras.t: Build HitCounter() with hit(t) (record a hit at second t) and getHits(t) (hits in the past 300 seconds, i.e. with timestamps in (t − 300, t]). Timestamps never decrease.
paras.s: Build Hit Counter with hit(t) (record a hit at second t) and get Hits(t) (hits in the past 300 seconds, that is with timestamps in (t minus 300, t ). Timestamps never decrease.

paras.t: Approach: Sliding Window Queue.
Hits arrive in time order, so keep their timestamps in a queue. Before answering, drop timestamps that slid out of the 300-second window from the front; the queue length is the answer.
Time O(1) amortised, space O(window).
paras.s: Time O of one amortised, space O of window.

paras.t: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) splits documents into overlapping chunks so no sentence is cut off from its context. Given tokens, a chunk size and an overlap (0 ≤ overlap < size), return the chunks: the first starts at index 0, each next chunk starts size − overlap tokens later, and you stop after the chunk that reaches the end. Return an empty list for empty input.
paras.s: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) splits documents into overlapping chunks so no sentence is cut off from its context. Given tokens, a chunk size and an overlap (0 less than or equal to overlap is less than size), return the chunks: the first starts at index 0, each next chunk starts size minus overlap tokens later, and you stop after the chunk that reaches the end. Return an empty list for empty input.

paras.t: Approach: Fixed Sliding Window.
A chunk is a window from left to right. Each step copies the window, then slides left forward by size − overlap, so the last overlap tokens are shared with the next chunk.
paras.s: A chunk is a window from left to right. Each step copies the window, then slides left forward by size minus overlap, so the last overlap tokens are shared with the next chunk.

paras.t: In production you'd chunk by tokens, not characters, and often snap boundaries to sentence ends.
Time O(n · size), space O(n · size).
paras.s: Time O of n times size, space O of n times size.

paras.t: An inference service logs request latencies in milliseconds. Return the average of every window of k consecutive latencies (one average per window, in order). This is how dashboards smooth noisy metrics.
Approach: Fixed Sliding Window.
Keep the sum of the current window. Add latencies[right]; once the window is longer than k, subtract latencies[left] and move left. Each full window contributes sum ÷ k.
paras.s: Keep the sum of the current window. Add latencies at right; once the window is longer than k, subtract latencies at left and move left. Each full window contributes sum divided by k.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1) extra.
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one extra.

paras.t: Protect a model endpoint: RateLimiter(limit, window) allows at most limit requests in any rolling window seconds. allow(t) is called with non-decreasing timestamps t (seconds) and returns true if the request at time t is accepted. A request at time p counts against t while t − p < window.
paras.s: Protect a model endpoint: Rate Limiter(limit, window) allows at most limit requests in any rolling window seconds. allow(t) is called with non-decreasing timestamps t (seconds) and returns true if the request at time t is accepted. A request at time p counts against t while t minus p is less than window.

paras.t: Approach: Sliding Window Log.
Keep a queue of accepted request times. Before each decision, pop times that are at least window seconds old; they slid out of the window.
If fewer than limit remain, accept and record the request. Each timestamp is pushed and popped once, so the cost is constant on average.
Time O(1) amortised, space O(limit). Compared with a fixed-window counter this never lets a burst through at the window boundary.
paras.s: Time O of one amortised, space O of limit. Compared with a fixed-window counter this never lets a burst through at the window boundary.

chapters.title: 185. Most Documents in a Context Budget

paras.t: Retrieved documents arrive in order with token counts tokens. You may send one contiguous run of them to the model, as long as their total stays within the context budget. Return the maximum number of documents you can send.
Approach: Sliding Window.
Add tokens[right] to the window. While the total exceeds the budget, drop documents from the left. The window is then a valid prompt, so compare its size with the best.
paras.s: Add tokens at right to the window. While the total exceeds the budget, drop documents from the left. The window is then a valid prompt, so compare its size with the best.

paras.t: Time O(n), space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of one.

paras.t: Semantic search compares a query embedding with stored vectors using cosine similarity (dot product divided by the product of lengths). Return the indices of the k most similar vectors, most similar first; break ties by smaller index. No vector is all zeros.
Approach: Min-Heap of Size k.
Compute each vector's cosine similarity with the query. Keep a min-heap holding the best k so far: if a new score beats the smallest in the heap, replace it.
At the end, sort the k survivors from most to least similar. Real vector databases replace this brute force with approximate indexes such as HNSW.
Time O(n · d + n log k), space O(k).
paras.s: Time O of n times d plus n log k, space O of k.

paras.t: Convert model logits into probabilities with softmax: p[i] = e^logits[i] / Σ e^logits[j]. Large logits like 1000 overflow exp, so make it numerically stable. Return the probabilities.
paras.s: Convert model logits into probabilities with softmax: p at i equals e to the power of logits at i divided by sigma e to the power of logits at j. Large logits like 1000 overflow exp, so make it numerically stable. Return the probabilities.

paras.t: Approach: Max-Shift Trick.
Softmax is unchanged if you subtract the same constant from every logit, because it cancels in the fraction. Subtract the maximum: now every exponent is at most 0, so exp can't overflow.
The same trick appears inside every attention layer of a transformer.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: Tokenizers like BPE learn merges: find the most frequent pair of adjacent tokens and fuse every occurrence into one token. Given tokens, count adjacent pairs (overlapping pairs count), pick the most frequent (ties: the pair that appears first), then merge its occurrences left to right without overlapping. Return the new token list; if there are fewer than two tokens, return it unchanged.
Approach: Count Pairs + Rebuild.
paras.s: Approach: Count Pairs plus Rebuild.

paras.t: One pass counts every adjacent pair and remembers where it first appears. The winner has the highest count, with earliest position breaking ties.
A second pass rebuilds the list: when the current token and the next form the winning pair, emit them fused and jump two steps.
Time O(n), space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of n, space O of n.

paras.t: To evaluate a retriever, compare its ranked results retrieved with the set of truly relevant document ids. Precision@k is the fraction of the top k results that are relevant. Return it as a decimal (if fewer than k results exist, still divide by k).
paras.s: To evaluate a retriever, compare its ranked results retrieved with the set of truly relevant document ids. Precision at k is the fraction of the top k results that are relevant. Return it as a decimal (if fewer than k results exist, still divide by k).

paras.t: Approach: Hash Set.
Load the relevant ids into a set. Walk the first k retrieved ids and count how many are in the set. Divide by k.
Pair it with recall@k (hits divided by the number of relevant docs) to see both sides of retrieval quality.
paras.s: Pair it with recall at k (hits divided by the number of relevant docs) to see both sides of retrieval quality.

paras.t: Time O(k + r), space O(r).
paras.s: Time O of k plus r, space O of r.

paras.t: A search index is split into shards. Each shard returns its scores sorted from highest to lowest. Merge them and return the n highest scores overall, highest first (fewer if there aren't enough).
Approach: Heap of Shard Fronts.
The next best score must be at the front of some shard. Put every shard's front into a max-heap. Pop the biggest, add it to the answer, and push the next score from the same shard.
This is the k-way merge used by distributed search engines and log aggregators.
Time O(n log s), space O(s).
paras.s: Time O of n log s, space O of s.

paras.t: Build LRUCache(capacity) with O(1) get(key) (return the value or -1) and put(key, value). When the cache is full, put of a new key evicts the least recently used key. Both get and put count as a use.
paras.s: Build LRUCache(capacity) with O of one get(key) (return the value or minus 1) and put(key, value). When the cache is full, put of a new key evicts the least recently used key. Both get and put count as a use.

paras.t: Approach: Hash Map + Ordered List.
paras.s: Approach: Hash Map plus Ordered List.

paras.t: Combine a hash map (instant lookup) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. Every use moves the entry to the newest end; eviction removes the oldest end.
Python's OrderedDict and Java's access-ordered LinkedHashMap are exactly this structure, so production code rarely hand-rolls it.
paras.s: Python's Ordered Dict and Java's access-ordered Linked Hash Map are exactly this structure, so production code rarely hand-rolls it.

paras.t: Time O(1) per call, space O(capacity). This is the classic answer behind CDN, database buffer-pool and LLM KV-cache eviction policies.
paras.s: Time O of one per call, space O of capacity. This is the classic answer behind CDN, database buffer-pool and LLM KV-cache eviction policies.

paras.t: Build LFUCache(capacity) with O(1) get(key) (value or -1) and put(key, value). When full, put of a new key evicts the key used the fewest times; among ties, evict the least recently used. A new key starts with one use.
paras.s: Build LFUCache(capacity) with O of one get(key) (value or minus 1) and put(key, value). When full, put of a new key evicts the key used the fewest times; among ties, evict the least recently used. A new key starts with one use.

paras.t: Approach: Frequency Buckets.
Keep each key's value and use count, plus one ordered bucket per count holding keys from least to most recent. Track min_freq, the smallest count present.
paras.s: Keep each key's value and use count, plus one ordered bucket per count holding keys from least to most recent. Track min freq, the smallest count present.

paras.t: A use moves a key from bucket f to bucket f + 1. Eviction removes the oldest key in the min_freq bucket.
paras.s: A use moves a key from bucket f to bucket f plus 1. Eviction removes the oldest key in the min freq bucket.

paras.t: Time O(1) per call, space O(capacity).
paras.s: Time O of one per call, space O of capacity.

paras.t: Implement TokenBucket(capacity, rate): the bucket starts full with capacity tokens and gains rate tokens per second (never exceeding capacity). allow(t) is called with non-decreasing whole-second timestamps; it refills the bucket for the elapsed time, then spends one token and returns true, or returns false if the bucket is empty.
paras.s: Implement Token Bucket(capacity, rate): the bucket starts full with capacity tokens and gains rate tokens per second (never exceeding capacity). allow(t) is called with non-decreasing whole-second timestamps; it refills the bucket for the elapsed time, then spends one token and returns true, or returns false if the bucket is empty.

paras.t: Approach: Lazy Refill.
Don't run a timer. On each call, add rate × elapsed seconds tokens, capped at capacity, then try to spend one.
paras.s: Don't run a timer. On each call, add rate times elapsed seconds tokens, capped at capacity, then try to spend one.

paras.t: Token buckets allow short bursts up to the capacity while enforcing the average rate. API gateways and LLM providers use them for per-key limits.
Time O(1) per call, space O(1).
paras.s: Time O of one per call, space O of one.

paras.t: Spread keys across cache servers so adding or removing a server moves few keys. Positions on a ring of 360 slots come from h(s) = Σ (i + 1) · code(s[i]) mod 360 (character codes, i from 0). Implement HashRing() with addNode(name), removeNode(name) and getNode(key): the owner is the first node at or clockwise after h(key), wrapping around. Node positions never collide in the tests, and getNode is only called when a node exists.
paras.s: Spread keys across cache servers so adding or removing a server moves few keys. Positions on a ring of 360 slots come from h of s equals sigma (i plus 1) times code(s at i) mod 360 (character codes, i from 0). Implement Hash Ring with add Node(name), remove Node(name) and get Node(key): the owner is the first node at or clockwise after h of key, wrapping around. Node positions never collide in the tests, and get Node is only called when a node exists.

paras.t: Approach: Sorted Ring + Binary Search.
paras.s: Approach: Sorted Ring plus Binary Search.

paras.t: Keep the node positions sorted. To place a key, binary search for the first node position at or after the key's hash; if none, wrap around to the first node.
Removing a node only moves the keys it owned to its clockwise neighbour, unlike hash mod N which reshuffles almost everything. Real systems add many virtual nodes per server to balance load.
Time O(log n) lookup, space O(n).
paras.s: Time O of log n lookup, space O of n.

paras.t: Protect callers from a failing dependency. CircuitBreaker(threshold, cooldown) starts "closed". record(t, ok) reports a call result at time t: success resets to "closed" with zero failures; a failure increments the failure count and trips the breaker "open" once failures reach threshold (or immediately when "half-open"). allow(t) returns whether a call may proceed: an "open" breaker turns "half-open" once cooldown seconds have passed since it opened. getState() returns the state.
paras.s: Protect callers from a failing dependency. Circuit Breaker(threshold, cooldown) starts "closed". record(t, ok) reports a call result at time t: success resets to "closed" with zero failures; a failure increments the failure count and trips the breaker "open" once failures reach threshold (or immediately when "half-open"). allow(t) returns whether a call may proceed: an "open" breaker turns "half-open" once cooldown seconds have passed since it opened. get State returns the state.

paras.t: Approach: State Machine.
Closed: calls flow and failures are counted. Open: calls are rejected immediately so the dependency can recover. Half-open: after the cooldown, a trial call decides whether to close again or reopen.
Libraries like Resilience4j implement exactly these transitions around remote calls.

Return the ID.

books.title: Computer Science Reviewer
books.author: Offleet
books.blurb: The core of a CS degree, condensed: complexity, data structures, algorithms, systems, networks, databases and theory.

paras.t: Big-O Notation: Big-O describes how an algorithm's cost grows as the input grows, ignoring constants.
paras.s: Big-O Notation. Big-O describes how an algorithm's cost grows as the input grows, ignoring constants. O of one constant, O of log n halving, O of n linear, O of n log n good sorting, O of n squared nested loops, O of 2 to the n explosive. Drop constants and smaller terms: 3n squared plus 5n plus 2 is O of n squared. Talk about worst case unless asked otherwise; mention average case for hashing and quicksort. Space complexity counts extra memory, including the recursion stack. In order from fastest to slowest: constant, logarithmic, linear, n log n, quadratic, exponential and factorial. Example: Two nested loops over n items do n times n equals n squared steps; one loop with a hash lookup inside is O of n. Remember: Ask yourself: how many times does the innermost line run as n doubles?

paras.t: Arrays vs Linked Lists: Arrays give instant index access; linked lists give cheap inserts once you're at the right node.
paras.s: Arrays versus Linked Lists. Arrays give instant index access; linked lists give cheap inserts once you're at the right node. Array: contiguous memory, O of one access by index, O of n insert or delete in the middle. Dynamic arrays (Array List, Python list) double their capacity, so append is O of one amortised. Linked list: O of one insert or delete given the node, but O of n to find a position. Arrays are cache-friendly; linked lists jump around memory. Example: Implementing an LRU cache uses a linked list for O of one move-to-front plus a hash map to find nodes. Remember: Need random access, use an array. Need lots of splicing at known spots, use a linked list.

paras.t: Hash Tables: A hash table maps keys to buckets with a hash function for average O(1) insert, lookup and delete.
paras.s: Hash Tables. A hash table maps keys to buckets with a hash function for average O of one insert, lookup and delete. The hash function turns a key into a bucket index. Collisions are handled by chaining (lists per bucket) or open addressing (probing). The load factor (items divided by buckets) triggers a resize to keep operations fast. Worst case is O of n when everything collides; good hashing makes that rare. Example: Two-sum in one pass: store each number's index in a map and look up target minus x. Remember: Keys must be immutable and have consistent equals and hash Code.

paras.t: Stacks, Queues and Deques: A stack is last-in-first-out, a queue is first-in-first-out, and a deque allows both ends.
paras.s: Stacks, Queues and Deques. A stack is last-in-first-out, a queue is first-in-first-out, and a deque allows both ends. Stack: push and pop at the top. Used for undo, call stacks, matching brackets and DFS. Queue: enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front. Used for BFS, task scheduling and buffering. Deque: push and pop at both ends in O of one, the basis of sliding-window maximums. In Java use Array Deque; in Python use collections.deque. Example: Checking uses a stack: push openers, pop and compare on closers. Remember: Recursion is an implicit stack; BFS needs an explicit queue.

paras.t: Heaps and Priority Queues: A binary heap keeps the smallest (or largest) item on top with O(log n) insert and remove.
paras.s: Heaps and Priority Queues. A binary heap keeps the smallest (or largest) item on top with O of log n insert and remove. Stored as an array: the children of index i are at 2i plus 1 and 2i plus 2. Push adds at the end and sifts up; pop moves the last item to the top and sifts down. Building a heap from n items takes O of n. Use it for top-k, scheduling, Dijkstra and merging sorted lists. Example: Keep a min-heap of size k to find the k largest items in O of n log k. Remember: Python's heapq is a min-heap; negate values for a max-heap.

paras.t: Trees and Binary Search Trees: A BST keeps smaller keys on the left and larger on the right, so search follows one path.
paras.s: Trees and Binary Search Trees. A BST keeps smaller keys on the left and larger on the right, so search follows one path. Traversals: pre-order (node first), in-order (sorted for a BST), post-order (children first), level-order (BFS). Balanced BSTs (red-black, AVL) guarantee O of log n operations; unbalanced ones can degrade to O of n. Height h bounds recursion depth and many costs. Java's Tree Map and C++'s std map are balanced BSTs. Example: An in-order walk of a BST prints its keys in sorted order. Remember: Tree problems usually reduce to: what should each node return to its parent?

paras.t: Graph Representations: Graphs model relationships: nodes (vertices) connected by edges, stored as lists or matrices.
paras.s: Graph Representations. Graphs model relationships: nodes (vertices) connected by edges, stored as lists or matrices. Adjacency list: O of V plus E space, best for sparse graphs (most real graphs). Adjacency matrix: O of V squared space, O of one edge checks, good for dense graphs. Edges can be directed or undirected, and weighted or unweighted. Trees are connected acyclic graphs; DAGs are directed acyclic graphs. Example: A social network with a billion users and a few hundred friends each needs adjacency lists. Remember: Ask early: directed? weighted? can it have cycles? is it connected?

paras.t: Sorting Algorithms: Comparison sorts can't beat O(n log n); merge sort, quicksort and heapsort reach it.
paras.s: Sorting Algorithms. Comparison sorts can't beat O of n log n; merge sort, quicksort and heapsort reach it. Merge sort: O of n log n always, stable, needs O of n extra memory. Quicksort: O of n log n on average, O of n squared worst case, in place and very fast in practice. Heapsort: O of n log n in place, not stable. Counting and radix sort beat n log n for small integer keys. Any comparison sort needs about n log n comparisons, because there are n factorial possible orders. Example: Java sorts objects with Tim Sort (a stable merge sort hybrid) and primitives with dual-pivot quicksort. Remember: Stable means equal keys keep their original order, which matters when sorting by several fields.

paras.t: Binary Search Beyond Arrays: Binary search works on any yes/no question that flips exactly once across a sorted range.
paras.s: Binary Search Beyond Arrays. Binary search works on any yes/no question that flips exactly once across a sorted range. Classic: find a value in a sorted array in O of log n. Lower bound: the first index where value greater than or equal to target. Search on the answer: the smallest capacity, speed or time that makes a check pass. Careful with mid equals (lo plus hi) over 2 overflow in Java; use lo plus (hi minus lo) over 2 or shifted right by >. Example: Smallest truck capacity that ships everything in D days: binary search capacities, check greedily. Remember: Decide whether your range is lo, hi or lo, hi) and stick to it.

paras.t: Recursion and Divide and Conquer: Solve a problem by solving smaller copies of it, then combining the answers.
paras.s: Recursion and Divide and Conquer. Solve a problem by solving smaller copies of it, then combining the answers. Every recursion needs a base case and progress toward it. Divide and conquer: split, solve the parts, combine (merge sort, quicksort, binary search). Master theorem: T of n equals aT(n/b) plus f of n gives the running time of many recurrences. Deep recursion can overflow the stack; convert to iteration if needed. Two half-size subproblems plus linear combining work gives n log n. Example: Merge sort splits in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges in linear time. Remember: Trust the recursion: assume the smaller call works and focus on combining.

paras.t: Dynamic Programming: DP solves overlapping subproblems once and reuses their answers.
paras.s: Dynamic Programming. DP solves overlapping subproblems once and reuses their answers. Two ingredients: optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Top-down: recursion plus memoization. Bottom-up: fill a table in dependency order. Define the state precisely, write the transition, set the base cases, then pick the answer cell. Often only the last row or last few values are needed, giving O of one or O of n space. Example: Climbing stairs: ways(n) equals ways(n minus 1) plus ways(n minus 2), with just two rolling variables. Remember: If brute force recomputes the same calls, cache them and you're doing DP.

paras.t: Greedy Algorithms: Greedy algorithms take the best-looking step now and never revisit it.
paras.s: Greedy Algorithms. Greedy algorithms take the best-looking step now and never revisit it. They work only when a local choice is provably part of some optimal solution. Classic wins: interval scheduling by earliest end, Huffman coding, Dijkstra, Kruskal. Prove it with an exchange argument: swapping in the greedy choice never makes things worse. When greedy fails, such as coin systems like 1, 3, 4 for amount 6, use DP. Example: To keep the most non-overlapping meetings, always pick the one that ends first. Remember: Try to break your greedy idea with a small counterexample before coding it.

paras.t: BFS vs DFS: BFS explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS dives deep first.
paras.s: BFS versus DFS. BFS explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS dives deep first. BFS uses a queue and visits nodes in order of distance. DFS uses recursion or a stack: good for connectivity, cycles, topological order and backtracking. Both run in O of V plus E with a visited set. On grids, neighbours are the 4 (or 8) adjacent cells. Example: Fewest moves for a knight on a chessboard: BFS. Count islands: DFS or BFS. Remember: Mark a node visited when you enqueue it, not when you dequeue it, to avoid duplicates.

paras.t: Shortest Paths: Dijkstra handles non-negative weights; Bellman-Ford handles negatives; Floyd-Warshall handles all pairs.
paras.s: Shortest Paths. Dijkstra handles non-negative weights; Bellman-Ford handles negatives; Floyd-Warshall handles all pairs. Dijkstra: a min-heap of (distance, node), O of E log V. Bellman-Ford: relax every edge V minus 1 times, O of V times E, and detects negative cycles. Floyd-Warshall: dynamic programming over intermediate nodes, O of V cubed. A times adds a heuristic to Dijkstra to aim at the goal faster. Example: Routing packets or maps with travel times: Dijkstra or A*. Remember: A negative edge breaks Dijkstra's assumption that a settled node is final.

paras.t: Topological Sort: A topological order lists a DAG's nodes so every edge points forward.
paras.s: Topological Sort. A topological order lists a DAG's nodes so every edge points forward. Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take nodes with in-degree 0. DFS version: record nodes after visiting their children, then reverse the list. If not every node gets output, the graph has a cycle. Used for build systems, course prerequisites and task scheduling. Example: Compile modules so each dependency is built before the modules that need it. Remember: A topological order exists if and only if the directed graph has no cycle.

paras.t: Processes vs Threads: Processes have separate memory; threads share their process's memory and are cheaper to create.
paras.s: Processes versus Threads. Processes have separate memory; threads share their process's memory and are cheaper to create. A process owns an address space, file handles and at least one thread. Threads share the heap, so they communicate easily but need synchronisation. Context switches between threads are cheaper than between processes. Java 21 virtual threads are cheap enough to create one per request. Example: A browser runs each tab in its own process so one crash doesn't take down the others. Remember: Isolation favours processes; cheap sharing favours threads.

paras.t: Race Conditions and Deadlocks: Races happen when timing changes results; deadlocks happen when threads wait on each other forever.
paras.s: Race Conditions and Deadlocks. Races happen when timing changes results; deadlocks happen when threads wait on each other forever. Race: two threads do read-modify-write on shared data without coordination. Fix races with locks, atomics, immutability or confinement to one thread. Deadlock needs four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Prevent deadlocks by always acquiring locks in a global order, or by using timeouts. Example: count++ is three steps (read, add, write); two threads can both read 5 and both write 6. Remember: Lock ordering is the simplest deadlock cure.

paras.t: Stack, Heap and Garbage Collection: The stack holds call frames; the heap holds objects that outlive a single call.
paras.s: Stack, Heap and Garbage Collection. The stack holds call frames; the heap holds objects that outlive a single call. Stack allocation is fast and freed automatically when a function returns. Heap objects are freed manually (C) or by a garbage collector (Java, Python, Go). Generational GC exploits the fact that most objects die young. Memory leaks in GC languages come from references you forgot to drop, such as caches and listeners. Example: A static Hash Map that only grows keeps every entry reachable, so it's never collected. Remember: Unbounded caches are leaks with good intentions: give them a size or time limit.

paras.t: Virtual Memory and Caching: Every process sees its own virtual address space; hardware maps pages to physical memory.
paras.s: Virtual Memory and Caching. Every process sees its own virtual address space; hardware maps pages to physical memory. Pages (often 4 KB) are mapped through page tables, sped up by the TLB. A page fault loads a page from disk when it isn't in memory. CPU caches (L1, L2, L3) exploit temporal and spatial locality. Sequential access through arrays is much faster than pointer chasing. Example: Iterating a 2D array row by row is faster than column by column in row-major languages. Remember: Rough latencies: L1 ~1 ns, RAM ~100 ns, SSD ~100 µs, a network round trip ~0.5 ms or more.

paras.t: TCP vs UDP: TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is fast, connectionless and best effort.
paras.s: TCP versus UDP. TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is fast, connectionless and best effort. TCP: three-way handshake, retransmissions, flow and congestion control. UDP: no handshake, no ordering, no retries; great for real-time media, games and DNS. QUIC (HTTP/3) builds reliability on top of UDP to avoid head-of-line blocking. Ports identify the application on a host. Example: A video call prefers a dropped frame over a late one, so it uses UDP or QUIC. Remember: Reliability costs latency; choose based on whether stale data is worse than missing data.
